pages.title: GLPI
pages.summary: Tickets (search, create, update, status, actors, follow-ups, tasks, solutions, attachments), assets, users and categories of a GLPI server, any API request, and a ticket trigger.
pages.html:
Rail22 connects to GLPI, the IT service management and asset software (GLPI 9.5 to 11), through its REST API (apirest.php). Its steps are in the Work management group of the step list:

  • GLPI Tickets: searches, reads, creates and updates tickets, changes their status, adds requesters, technicians, groups and observers, follow-ups, tasks, solutions and attachments, deletes them.
  • GLPI Assets: the inventory's items of any type (computers, monitors, network equipment, printers, phones, software, …): lists, searches, reads, creates, updates and deletes them.
  • GLPI Setup: users, groups, entities, categories, locations, and the search engine's field numbers.
  • GLPI API: any request of the REST API, such as problems, changes, contracts or validations.

The GLPI ticket trigger starts a workflow when tickets are created or updated.

The credential

In GLPI, the API has to be on: Setup > General > API, Enable Rest API. There, an API client lists the addresses allowed to use it, and can have an App-Token. Then, under Credentials & variables, create a GLPI credential, in the Work management group. The steps act as that user, with the rights of its profile in GLPI: a user made for Rail22 keeps its changes easy to tell apart.

SettingDescription
ServerThe address you open GLPI at, such as https://glpi.example.com or https://example.com/glpi. HTTPS only.
Sign in withThe user's API token (in GLPI: My settings > Remote access keys > API token), or Login and password (the API client must allow signing in with credentials).
App-TokenThe API client's, when it has one. Stored encrypted, as the token and the password are.
Profile ID, Entity IDThe profile and the entity to work in, such as profile 6 (Technician) and entity 0 (the root), with or without its sub-entities. Empty: the user's defaults.
Trust the server's certificateOnly for a self-signed certificate.

Test shows the user, its profile and entity. A server on a private address (inside your network) needs the account's Integrations may connect to private network addresses. Each step opens a session of the API and closes it when it ends.

What the steps share

  • Tickets and items are given by id (12), by address (…/front/ticket.form.php?id=12), or as a ticket of a search or of the trigger, so {{ item }} in a loop, or {{ ticket }}, names it.
  • A ticket is { id, url, name, content, status, statusId, type, urgency, impact, priority, category, entity, location, requestType, date, date_mod, date_creation, solvedate, closedate, fields }. status is New, Processing (assigned), Processing (planned), Pending, Solved or Closed (statusId 1 to 6); content is plain text; fields has every field as GLPI gives it. Dates are in the GLPI server's time zone.
  • Texts (descriptions, follow-ups, tasks, solutions) are plain text: paragraphs at blank lines. GLPI stores them as HTML: Rail22 converts them both ways. A text with HTML tags is sent as it is.
  • Users are given by login, by email or by id; groups, categories, entities, locations and statuses by id, by name or by complete name (Hardware > Printers). Two of the same name: give the complete name or the id.
  • Lists give { items, count, truncated }, at most At most (items).
  • Searches can add GLPI's own search criteria, a JSON list such as [{"field": 7, "searchtype": "equals", "value": 3}], where field is the number of a search option: GLPI Setup's List search options gives them.
  • Errors: GLPI's message, with its code, such as Mandatory fields are not filled. Please correct: Title (ERROR_GLPI_ADD). With On error set to continue, the step goes on through its error output.

Note: for an AI step, creating, changing and deleting tickets and items are write operations: not offered by default, and they ask for approval when approvals are on.

pages.title: GLPI Tickets
pages.summary: Searches, reads, creates and updates tickets; status, actors, follow-ups, tasks, solutions, attachments.
pages.html:
The GLPI Tickets step works with the helpdesk's tickets.

The credential, the results and the errors are the same for every GLPI step: see GLPI.

Operations

OperationGLPI REST APIResult
Search ticketssearch/Ticket, getMultipleItems{ items, count, truncated }: the tickets of a status (by default Not solved or closed) whose title has Title contains, and that GLPI's Criteria find, the newest updated first (or by date of opening).
Get a ticketTicket/<id>The ticket, with its actors: requesters, assigned, observers, each a list of { kind, name, email }, kind being user, group or email.
Create a ticketPOST TicketThe new ticket. A title and a description are required. The requester can be an email of no GLPI user: GLPI notifies that address. Other fields go in Other fields, such as {"locations_id": 3}.
Update a ticketPUT Ticket/<id>The ticket. The settings that are not empty are changed.
Change the statusPUT Ticket/<id>The ticket. A follow-up can go with it (Text), such as the reason it waits.
Add an actorTicket_User, Group_Ticket{ id, role, user, group, changes }: a user and / or a group added as Assigned to, Requester or Observer. One already there is not added again. Replace the others removes the other users (groups) of that role: a ticket handed over.
Add a follow-upPOST ITILFollowup{ id, ticket, content, private }.
List follow-upsTicket/<id>/ITILFollowup{ items, count, truncated }: the newest first, each with date, user, content (plain text), private.
Add a taskPOST TicketTask{ id, ticket, content, private }: with its duration, state (to do, done, information) and technician.
List tasksTicket/<id>/TicketTask{ items, count, truncated }: the newest first, with state, duration (minutes) and technician too.
Add a solutionPOST ITILSolution{ id, ticket, status }. GLPI marks the ticket Solved (or Closed, as the entity's settings say).
Attach a filePOST Document{ id, name, size, ticket }: a project file, such as {{ file.id }}, added as a document of the ticket.
Delete a ticketDELETE Ticket/<id>{ id, deleted, purged }: to the trash, or for good with Purge.

SettingDescription
GLPI credentialA GLPI credential of the project. Required.
OperationChoices: Search tickets; Get a ticket; Create a ticket; Update a ticket; Change the status; Add an actor; Add a follow-up; List follow-ups; Add a task; List tasks; Add a solution; Attach a file; Delete a ticket. Default: Search tickets. Required.
StatusChoices: Any; Not solved or closed; Not closed; Processing; Solved or closed; New; Processing (assigned); Processing (planned); Pending; Solved; Closed. Default: Not solved or closed. (For: Search tickets.)
Title contains(For: Search tickets.)
OrderChoices: The newest updated first; The newest first; The oldest first. Default: The newest updated first. (For: Search tickets.)
CriteriaGLPI's search criteria, a JSON list added to those above, e.g. [{"field": 7, "searchtype": "equals", "value": 3}] (the fields' numbers: GLPI Setup, List search options). (For: Search tickets.)
TicketIts id, its address, or a ticket of a search or a trigger. (Required for: Get a ticket, Update a ticket, Change the status, Add an actor, Add a follow-up, List follow-ups, Add a task, List tasks, Add a solution, Attach a file, Delete a ticket.)

DescriptionPlain text (paragraphs at blank lines) or HTML; required to create. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
TypeChoices: (GLPI's default / unchanged); Incident; Request. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
UrgencyChoices: (GLPI's default / unchanged); Very low; Low; Medium; High; Very high. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
ImpactChoices: (GLPI's default / unchanged); Very low; Low; Medium; High; Very high. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
PriorityChoices: (from urgency and impact / unchanged); Very low; Low; Medium; High; Very high; Major. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
CategoryIts id or complete name, e.g. Hardware > Printers. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
EntityIts id or complete name; empty: the session's. (For: Create a ticket.)
RequesterA login, an email or a user id; an email of no user is notified. Empty: GLPI's default (often the API user). (For: Create a ticket.)
Assigned toA login, an email or a user id. Add an actor: the user (or a group) to add. (For: Create a ticket, Add an actor.)
GroupAssigned to: a group's id or complete name. (For: Create a ticket, Add an actor.)
Other fieldsA JSON object merged into the input, as GLPI names the fields, e.g. {"locations_id": 3, "requesttypes_id": 1}. (For: Create a ticket, Update a ticket.)
AsChoices: Assigned to; Requester; Observer. Default: Assigned to. (Required for: Add an actor.)
Replace the othersThe ticket's other users (groups) of that role removed. Default: off. (For: Add an actor.)
New statusChoices: New; Processing (assigned); Processing (planned); Pending; Solved; Closed. Default: Processing (assigned). (Required for: Change the status.)
TextPlain text or HTML. Change the status: optional, a follow-up added with it. (Required for: Add a follow-up, Add a task, Add a solution.)
PrivateSeen by the technicians only. Default: off. (For: Change the status, Add a follow-up, Add a task.)
Duration (minutes)Default: 0. (For: Add a task.)
StateChoices: To do; Done; Information. Default: Done. (For: Add a task.)
TechnicianA login, an email or a user id; empty: the API user. (For: Add a task.)
Solution typeIts id or name; empty: none. (For: Add a solution.)
Project fileThe id of a file of the project, e.g. {{ file.id }}. (Required for: Attach a file.)
Largest size (MB)Default: 10. (Required for: Attach a file.)
PurgeDeleted for good; off: to the trash. Default: off. (For: Delete a ticket.)
At most (items)Of a list: more are left out (truncated). Default: 100. Required. (For: Search tickets, List follow-ups, List tasks.)
Timeout (s)Default: 60. Required.
Result variableA list: { items, count, truncated }; otherwise what the operation gives. Default: tickets. Required.
On errorGLPI's errors, or no connection. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the error output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

For example, alerts as tickets: a monitoring trigger, then Search tickets for an open one (Title contains {{ alert.host }}); when {{ tickets.count }} is 0, Create a ticket in the right category and group, else Add a follow-up. When the alert clears, Add a solution.

pages.title: Microsoft Intune
pages.summary: Devices (filters, remote actions: sync, restart, lock, wipe, retire), compliance policies and configuration profiles, apps and their assignments, Windows Autopilot, any Graph request, and a device trigger.
pages.html:
Rail22 connects to Microsoft Intune through Microsoft Graph, as an app of your tenant: no user signs in, so workflows don't stop when someone's session ends. Its steps are in the Microsoft group of the step list:

  • Intune Devices: lists the managed devices by operating system, compliance, ownership, user, name or serial number; reads one, its apps and compliance states; sends remote actions (sync, restart, lock, shut down, locate, reset the passcode, Defender scan and signatures, retire, wipe); deletes it.
  • Intune Policies: compliance policies and configuration profiles, their assignments, their devices' statuses and their counts.
  • Intune Apps: the apps Intune deploys and their assignments (adds and removes them), and the apps found on the devices.
  • Intune Autopilot: Windows Autopilot devices: imports them by hardware hash, sets their group tag and user, deletes them.
  • Intune API: any Microsoft Graph request as the app, such as the settings catalog, scripts or update rings (Graph beta).

The Intune device trigger starts a workflow when devices are enrolled or become noncompliant.

The credential

In the Microsoft Entra admin center, under App registrations, register an app (single tenant). Under Certificates & secrets, make a client secret and copy its Value. Under API permissions, add the Microsoft Graph application permissions the steps you use need, then Grant admin consent:

StepsApplication permission
Intune Devices (reading), discovered apps, the Intune device trigger, the credential's TestDeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All
Intune Devices: remote actions (sync, restart, lock, wipe, retire, …)DeviceManagementManagedDevices.PrivilegedOperations.All
Intune Devices: deleteDeviceManagementManagedDevices.ReadWrite.All
Intune PoliciesDeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All
Intune AppsDeviceManagementApps.Read.All; to assign: DeviceManagementApps.ReadWrite.All
Intune AutopilotDeviceManagementServiceConfig.Read.All; to import, update, delete: DeviceManagementServiceConfig.ReadWrite.All

Then, under Credentials & variables, create a Microsoft Intune credential, in the Microsoft group:

SettingDescription
TenantThe tenant ID (Entra admin center > Overview) or its domain, such as contoso.onmicrosoft.com.
Client IDThe app's Application (client) ID.
Client secretThe secret's value. Stored encrypted. A secret expires: make a new one in time, and update the credential.

Test shows how many devices are enrolled, by operating system. Intune's audit log names the app for what the steps do: give it a name that says so, such as Rail22 workflows.

What the steps share

  • Devices are given by id, as a device of a list or of the trigger ({{ device }}), or by name or serial number, when exactly one device has it. Policies and apps are given by id or by name.
  • A device is { id, url, name, user, userName, email, os, osVersion, compliance, ownership, model, manufacturer, serialNumber, enrolled, lastSync, encrypted, azureADDeviceId, managementAgent, fields }. url opens it in the Intune admin center; compliance is compliant, noncompliant, inGracePeriod, …; ownership company or personal; times are in UTC; fields has every field as Graph gives it.
  • Remote actions are sent to Intune, which passes them to the device at its next check-in: the result says the action was sent, not done.
  • Lists give { items, count, truncated }, at most At most (items).
  • Errors: Graph's message, with its code, such as Defender scan is only supported on Windows devices (BadRequest). A missing permission is HTTP status 403. When Graph throttles (HTTP status 429), the step waits and sends the request again, within its Timeout. With On error set to continue, the step goes on through its error output.

Note: for an AI step, the remote actions, deletes, assignments and Autopilot changes are write operations: not offered by default, and they ask for approval when approvals are on. Keep Wipe and Retire behind an approval.

pages.title: Intune Devices

pages.title: Expressions
pages.summary: Using the data of earlier steps in settings: {{ }} expressions, fields, lists, methods and project variables.
pages.html:
Most step settings accept expressions: pieces between {{ and }} that are replaced, when the step runs, by values from the run. The language is a safe subset of JavaScript.

Hello {{ form_user.name }}, your order {{ order.number }} is confirmed.

Text or value

  • A setting that is only one expression (spaces around are fine) gives the value as it is: a number, a list, an object. {{ response.body.items }} is the list itself.
  • A setting with text around expressions gives text. Lists and objects are written as JSON, and an empty value as nothing.

Reaching into data

ExpressionGives
{{ mail.subject }}A field of an object
{{ mail.headers["x-priority"] }}A field whose name has dashes or spaces
{{ mails[0].from }}The first item of a list (positions start at 0)
{{ mails.length }}The number of items
{{ response.body?.data?.id }}Nothing, instead of an error, when a part is missing
{{ vars.support_email }}A project variable

Computing

{{ order.quantity * order.price }}
{{ mail.subject.toUpperCase() }}
{{ mail.from.split("@")[1] }}
{{ response.status === 200 ? "ok" : "failed" }}
{{ form.comment ?? "no comment" }}
{{ table.rows.filter(r => r.status === "open").length }}
{{ table.rows.map(r => r.email).join(", ") }}
{{ Math.round(total * 100) / 100 }}
{{ Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10) }}

Strings, lists and numbers have the usual JavaScript methods: trim, includes, replace, slice, filter, map, find, join, toFixed… plus Math, JSON, Date and regular expressions. Write Date() without new. Dates come out as ISO 8601 text.

Help while typing

In expression fields the designer suggests, after {{, the variables available at that step: those set by the trigger and the steps before it, with their fields and types. It also marks mistakes: an unclosed {{, a syntax error, or a name no earlier step sets.

Where variables come from

  • The trigger: webhook, form, file, mail, schedule_time.
  • Each step's result variable: response, table, ai, task…
  • Set and Code steps, which set variables you name.
  • Inside a loop: item and index.
  • The project variables, always: vars.<name>.

Variables live as long as the run. A later step that sets the same name replaces the value.

Limits

An expression runs in a sandbox: it can only read the run's variables, and it stops if it runs too long (one second). An expression that fails, for example by calling a method on nothing, fails its step, with the reason in the execution's error. Use ?. and ?? for values that may be missing.

The full language reference is in The expression language.

pages.title: Errors, limits and timeouts
pages.summary: What happens when a step fails, how to handle errors in the workflow, and the limits of a run.
pages.html:
When a step fails

By default, a step that fails stops the run. The execution's state becomes Error, with the step's name and the reason, such as HTTP Request: status 503, a timeout, a missing credential, or an expression that failed. The steps after it don't run.

Handling errors in the workflow

Steps that call other systems (HTTP Request, Download File, FTP, Data Table, Code, the AI and integration steps) have an On error setting:

  • Fail the step (default): the run stops, as above.
  • Continue on the error output: the step gets two outputs, success and error. On a failure, the run continues on error, and the result variable tells what went wrong: response.status and response.error, ai.error, table.error, or error for Code.

From the error output you can retry after a Wait, notify someone, log the problem in a data table, or take another way.

In a Loop, On error in a pass = Skip the item and continue keeps one bad item from stopping the others. The skipped items are listed in loop.errors.

Timeouts

StepDefault timeout
HTTP Request30 s
Download File, FTP / SFTP (per file)120 s
Google and Microsoft steps60 s (Google Drive, OneDrive / SharePoint: 120 s)
AI steps (per call to the model)300 s (at most 600); Lemonade AI, LM Studio and Ollama, on local servers: 900 s (at most 900)
Code5 s (at most 30)

Limits of a run

  • A run executes at most 10,000 steps, counting each pass of a loop. This protects against endless loops.
  • A loop takes at most 1000 items.
  • An execution keeps the last 500 log lines.
  • An expression may run for one second at most.
  • A webhook request body is at most 1 MB.
  • A caller waits at most 30 seconds for a run's result (a webhook set to answer When the workflow ends, the MCP run_workflow tool). After that it gets the state queued, and the run goes on.

Account limits

Your account's plan may limit the number of data tables, the rows in one table, the size of all files, and the System AI credits per month. The Usage tab of Account settings (Settings menu) shows where you stand. A step that would go over a limit fails with a message saying which one.

pages.title: Publishing and versions
pages.summary: Drafts and published versions: publishing, unpublishing, viewing and restoring versions.
pages.html:
A workflow has one draft, the version you edit, and any number of published versions: v1, v2, v3… At most one of them is published at a time, and that is the one the trigger runs.

Publishing

  1. Open the status menu in the toolbar. It says Draft, or v2 published.
  2. Choose Publish the draft as v3, the next number.
  3. Add a note, such as "retry on 503", then confirm.

The draft must have no errors. The new version becomes the published one right away, and the trigger starts using it: the schedule, webhook, form, file upload or email address.

You can also publish and unpublish from the three-dots menu next to a workflow in the sidebar. Published workflows have a green dot.

Some triggers also set up the other system when the workflow is published: the GravityZone event trigger, with Connect on, points GravityZone's push service to the workflow. A message after publishing says how it went. A failure there doesn't undo the publishing.

Tests before publishing

If the workflow has test cases, the Publish dialog shows the latest result. With Tests must pass to publish on, in the Tests panel, a new version of the draft is refused unless the latest test run passed on this same draft and these same test cases. Moving a step on the canvas or editing a note doesn't count as a change; changing anything else does, so run the tests again. A workflow with no test cases can't be published while the setting is on.

Only a new version of the draft is held back. Publish again on an older version, and publishing an unchanged draft again, stay open, so that you can always roll back.

Working on a published workflow

Editing changes only the draft. The toolbar shows draft changed, and the trigger keeps running the published version until you publish again. So you can work on a live workflow safely, test the draft with Run, and publish when ready.

Unpublishing

Unpublish stops the trigger from starting new runs. Runs already in progress finish. The version is kept: if the draft has not changed, Publish v3 makes it live again.

Unpublishing a workflow with a GravityZone event trigger turns GravityZone's push service off, if it still points to this workflow. So does publishing a version without that trigger.

Versions

Versions, in the status menu, lists every published version with its date, who published it and its note. Open one to see it on the canvas, read-only. From there:

  • Publish again: makes that version the published one, for example to roll back quickly.
  • Copy into the draft: replaces the draft with that version, to continue from it.
  • Duplicate: creates a new workflow from it.
  • Back to the draft: returns to editing.

Duplicating and deleting

Both are in the workflow's three-dots menu in the sidebar and in its version menu in the designer. Duplicate creates a new workflow from the saved draft, unpublished. Delete removes the workflow with all its versions and executions. This cannot be undone.

Moving to another project

In the workflow's three-dots menu in the sidebar, or its version menu in the designer, Move to project takes it to another project, with its versions, runs, tests, tasks, conversations and the state of its triggers. Its trigger addresses and tokens stay the same, and a published workflow stays published, so it goes on starting runs in the new project. You need permission to delete it in its project and to create it in the new one, and to publish there if it is published. Personal projects cannot receive it. It cannot move while it has runs in progress or waiting, or while its tests are running. It keeps its shares with other projects; a share with the new project ends. The old project's logs and the files its runs saved stay where they are.

The dialog names what to fix before you move. The credentials, data tables, knowledge bases, variables and called workflows it uses stay in the old project: those steps fail in the new one until they are moved, shared with it or made again there. Workflows of the old project that call it fail at that step until they are changed or the new project shares it back.

Sharing with other projects

A published workflow that starts with Called by a workflow can be shared with other projects of the account. In its menu, in the sidebar or the designer, click Share and choose a project. That project can then call it with the Run a workflow step, or give it to an AI step as a tool.

  • Where it runs: in its own project, with that project's credentials, tables and variables. The caller gives the inputs and gets the outputs, the state, the error if it fails, and the execution's id.
  • Which version: always the published one. Changes to the draft reach no one until you publish. If you unpublish it, or stop sharing it, calls fail at that step.
  • What the other project sees: under Shared workflows in the sidebar: its description, inputs, outputs and step names. Not its settings, runs or tests, and it cannot change or copy it. People who need more should be members of the workflow's project.
  • Changing what it takes or returns: the Publish dialog warns when a new version changes its inputs or outputs, and names the workflows that call it.
  • Who can share: the permission Share workflows, which only Owners have by default. Seeing a shared workflow needs See what workflows shared with the project offer, which Owners and Members have. Personal projects neither share nor receive.
  • Deleting: a workflow cannot be deleted while it is shared. The Share dialog shows which workflows use it in each project.

The MCP server does not list or start workflows of other projects.

pages.title: Executions
pages.summary: Following runs in the designer, reading their log and variables, and the account's execution log.
pages.html:
Each run of a workflow is an execution. It records what started it, the version it ran (or the draft), its state, its log and its variables.

The Executions panel

In the designer, click the clock icon, or press Run, which opens the panel on the new run. The panel lists the workflow's executions, newest first, and refreshes every few seconds. Select one to see:

  • The state, what started it (manual, webhook, schedule…) and the version.
  • The error, if the run failed: the step and the reason.
  • The log: one line per step, with the time, plus the lines your Code steps write with console.log.
  • The agent trace of each AI step, if the run has any: see below.
  • The variables at the end of the run, or at its current point if it is still running. This is the quickest way to see what each step produced. Each variable is one line: click an object or a list to open it, and click it again to close it. What you open stays open while the panel refreshes.

The run on the canvas

The execution you select in the panel is also shown on the canvas, and follows the run live. When you open a workflow, the latest run that is still running or sleeping is shown by itself, even with the panel closed. A chip at the top of the canvas says which run is shown: click it to open that run in the panel, or click its x to take the marks off. Selecting a run in the panel shows it again.

  • A green tick marks the steps that are done, and the connections the run went through. A step that ran several times, such as one inside a Loop, says how many times when you point at its tick.
  • A blue play icon marks the step running now. The connection that led to it moves.
  • An amber pause icon marks a Wait step waiting for its time, an hourglass a Merge waiting for its other inputs.
  • A red cross marks the step that failed, a grey stop icon the step a killed run was at.
  • Steps and connections the run has not reached have no mark, such as the branch an If did not take.

The marks stay when you close the panel. A run of a published version is shown on the draft's canvas: steps added or removed since have no mark.

The agent trace

An AI step leaves a trace of each visit, so you can see why the agent did what it did. A step inside a Loop has one per pass, numbered after the step's name. The panel shows the trace above the log, and follows a run live.

Each trace starts with one line: its state, the model, the rounds and tool calls, the tokens (input + output), the cost, and how long it took. Open it for its rounds, one per call to the model, closed at first:

  • A round shows the model, its tokens and cost, how long it took, and the text the model gave, if any.
  • A tool call opens on its arguments and result. It says whether the tool only reads or is a write, how long it ran, and if it failed.
  • An approval shows on its call: waiting, approved or rejected and by whom, when, with the comment of a rejection, or not approved in time. See Approvals.

What the panel can show has limits:

  • Long texts are cut, and the panel says how long the full text was: the model's text at 20,000 characters, a tool's result and a call's arguments at 8,000 each. Past about 4 MB in one trace, each further text is cut at 500 characters. The model itself got up to 50,000 characters of a result.
  • Secrets are removed: arguments named like one (password, token, API key and the like), their form inside a text (bearer tokens, private keys, passwords in URLs, password: …), and the values of the credentials the step uses, wherever they turn up. A secret with no such sign cannot be caught.
  • With Mask personal data on, the trace holds what the model saw: placeholders, not the real values. The step's variable and the audit log have the real ones.
  • The cost is an estimate, from the tokens and the prices in use, or the credits used on the System AI. Without a known price it says so: see AI steps.

Anyone who can open the workflow can read its traces. A trace goes when its execution is deleted, and also after the time set in Keep execution log entries in Account settings, whichever comes first, even if the execution itself stays. One still waiting for an approval is kept until it ends.

Running again with the same inputs

To compare a change, such as a new prompt, select a finished execution and click the Run again icon (two arrows), then confirm. You need to be allowed to edit the workflow. Your changes are saved first. A new execution starts with the same trigger and the same inputs, and says which execution it ran again.

  • It runs the current draft, whichever version the first run used.
  • Everything runs again, tools and write operations included, and it costs what a run costs. Approvals are asked again.
  • It is refused if the workflow has errors, or if its trigger is no longer of the same type: the inputs would not fit.
  • A workflow started by Run a workflow runs on its own: the workflow that called it is not resumed again.

States

StateMeaning
NewStarted, waiting for its turn.
RunRunning now.
SleepWaiting for a Wait step's time or a human task. It continues by itself.
CompletedFinished without errors.
ErrorA step failed. The error says which and why.
CancelledKilled by someone. The error says who.

Runs started by other runs

A run started by a Run a workflow step is an execution of the workflow it started, with the trigger call. Its log names the run that started it, and the starting run's log names the execution it started. A run that waits for another one shows as sleeping until it ends; killing it kills the run it waits for.

Saving a run as a test case

To check later that the workflow still handles a run like this one, select the finished run and click Save as test case (the clipboard icon with the plus). See Testing AI steps.

Killing a run

To stop a run that is new, running or sleeping, select it and click the red stop icon, then confirm. You need to be allowed to edit the workflow. The run becomes Cancelled. It stops at once. Long runs can also be killed from the Overview.

Cleaning up

Executions of the draft, from Run, can be deleted from the panel, one at a time or all at once. Executions of published versions, and those still running or sleeping, are kept. Their lines in the execution log stay in any case.

The execution log

Besides each workflow's executions, the account keeps an execution log of all runs and of the requests refused by triggers, such as a webhook call with a wrong secret. Owners find it in the Settings menu under System execution log. How long entries are kept is an account setting.

The Overview page shows the runs of the last days, with how many completed and how many failed.

pages.title: Modeling a workflow
pages.summary: Thinking a workflow through before drawing it: outcome, the six questions, building blocks, data, naming, running twice, failures, testing.
pages.html:
A workflow is a model of a piece of work: what starts it, what it needs to know, what it decides, who takes part, and what it leaves behind. This page is about thinking a workflow through before you draw it. A good model is easier to build, to test and to change later. For the steps themselves, see Steps.

Start from the outcome

Write down, in one sentence, what is true when the workflow has done its job. For example: "Every expense request has a decision, the employee knows it, and the request is recorded." Then work backwards: which steps make that true, and what does each of them need?

Write down also what is not the workflow's job. A workflow that does one thing well is easier to follow than one that handles every case of a department.

The six questions

Most workflows can be described by answering six questions. Each answer maps to a part of Rail22:

QuestionIn Rail22
What starts it? An event, a time, a person.The trigger: Webhook, Schedule, Form, File upload, Email, Manual.
What data comes in, and what data is needed?The trigger's variable (form, webhook, mail…), plus lookups: HTTP Request, Data Table, the database steps, LDAP.
What is decided?If and Switch, with expressions. AI steps for decisions that need judgment.
Who takes part?Human tasks for decisions and reviews, Forms for requests, emails for information.
What waits, and for how long?Wait, a Human task's time limit, a Schedule that comes back later.
What must be remembered after the run?Data tables, files, or the other system the workflow writes to.

One more question is easy to forget: what can go wrong? An API that does not answer, a row that does not exist, a person who never completes the task. See Plan for failures below.

Sketch it first

Before opening the designer, sketch the path as a list or a few boxes. It does not need to be pretty. For an expense approval:

Form: amount, reason
  → record the request (status: pending)
  → ask a manager: approve or reject?        (waits for a person)
      → record the decision
      → approved?  yes → email "approved" to the employee
                   no  → email "rejected", with the manager's comment

Each arrow becomes a connection, each line a step. The sketch already shows the If after the task, and that the request is saved before the run waits, so it is recorded even if nobody answers. The full version is in Example: expense approval.

Building blocks

Sequence

Steps connected one after another run in order. Each step can use the variables of every step before it.

Decision

An If continues on true or false. A Switch picks one of several outputs. Prefer one Switch to a chain of Ifs when the same value is tested several times.

Join

A Merge brings branches back together, so the steps after it are drawn once, not on each branch.

Repetition

A Loop runs the steps inside it for each item of a list: the emails read, the rows found, the items of an API response. Decide what happens when one item fails: stop everything, or skip it and continue.

Waiting

A run can wait for a time or for a person without using resources: it sleeps and continues later. Model long processes (days, weeks) as one run that waits, not as a run that loops and checks.

People

A Human task is a step like any other: it has a form, and its answers become variables. Give it a clear name with expressions (Approve {{ form.amount }} EUR) so the person knows what to do from the task list alone.

Reusing workflows

When several workflows repeat the same steps, move them into one workflow that starts with Called by a workflow, declare what it needs (inputs) and what it gives back (outputs), and run it with Run a workflow. Fix it once, and every workflow that uses it gets the fix when you publish it.

Data: variables or tables

Every run has its own variables. They hold what the trigger received and what each step produced, and they are gone for the next run. Keep in variables what only this run needs.

What must outlive the run, or be shared between runs and workflows, goes into a data table: the requests and their status, the emails already handled, a list of customers, a mapping from a code to an address. Values that rarely change and are the same for every run, such as a base URL or a team's address, are project variables ({{ vars.name }}).

Keep it inWhenExample
A run variableOnly this run needs it.The API response, the AI answer, the task's decision.
A project variableA setting, the same for every run.vars.api_base, vars.finance_email.
A data tableRecords that grow, change, or are looked up.Requests, tickets, products, processed message ids.
FilesDocuments.Attachments, generated PDFs, uploads.

Using data tables covers designing tables and the usual patterns.

Name things well

  • Result variables: give each step a variable named after what it holds. Two Data Table steps both write table by default, and the second replaces the first. customer, ticket and open_orders read better in later expressions and cannot collide.
  • Steps: rename them after what they do: Find customer, Record ticket, Notify support. The executions' log then reads like a story.
  • Table columns: the column key is what expressions use ({{ customer.row.email }}), and it cannot be changed later. Choose short, lower-case keys.

Make it safe to run twice

A trigger may fire again for the same thing: a webhook sent twice by the other system, an email read again, a run started by hand to test. A good workflow gives the same result when that happens. This property is called idempotency. The usual ways:

  • Record what was handled, keyed by an id from the source (an order number, the email's message_id), with Insert or update on that column instead of Insert.
  • Check before acting: query the table for the id, and continue with an If only when nothing was found.
  • Use a status column (pending, done) and only pick rows that are still pending.

Several runs of the same workflow may also run at the same time. Do not count on a value read at the start of a run still being the same at its end, for example a counter read, increased and written back by two runs at once.

Plan for failures

By default a step that fails stops the run, and the execution shows the error. That is often right: a run that stops is easy to see and to start again. Where another path is better, steps that call other systems have an On error setting: Continue on the error output lets you connect a fallback, such as an email to an administrator, or a row with status failed. See Errors, limits and timeouts.

  • Order the steps so that a failure leaves things consistent. Delete old rows after the new ones are saved, not before.
  • Give Human tasks a time limit when someone must act in time, and connect the timeout output to a reminder or an escalation.
  • In a Loop over many items, Skip the item and continue keeps one bad item from stopping the rest. The skipped ones are listed in loop.errors.

Test as you build

  1. Build the first few steps and press Run. With a Manual trigger, set test values with a Set step at the start.
  2. Open the run in Executions: check the log and the variables each step produced. Expressions in the next steps are easier to write once you have seen the real data.
  3. Add the next steps, run again. Test the unhappy paths too: an empty list, a missing row, a rejected request.
  4. Publish when it works. The trigger starts only the published version, so you can keep improving the draft.

Checklist

  • The outcome fits in one sentence.
  • Every input the workflow needs comes from the trigger, a lookup, or a project variable.
  • Every decision has both of its sides connected, or deliberately ends there.
  • Result variables have names that say what they hold.
  • Running it twice for the same input does no harm.
  • What happens on failure, and who finds out, is decided.
  • Records that must outlive the run are in a data table.

pages.title: Using data tables
pages.summary: Designing data tables and using them from workflows: columns, relations, reading and writing rows, and the usual patterns.
pages.html:
A data table is a simple table kept inside Rail22: columns you define, rows that workflows and people add. This guide is about designing tables and using them from workflows. For the screens, see Data tables. For every setting of the step, see Data Table step.

When to use a data table

Use a data table for what a workflow must remember between runs, or share with other workflows and with people:

  • Records the process creates: requests, tickets, orders, sign-ups.
  • Status: which requests are pending, approved, done.
  • Reference data to look up: customers, products, a mapping from a country to a sales manager.
  • Memory: the ids of the emails or orders already handled, so they are not handled twice.
  • Logs: one row per run or per item, to review or export later.

A data table is not meant to replace your main database or ERP. When the data already lives in another system, read it from there (HTTP Request, a database step) and keep in a table only what the workflow itself needs.

Designing a table

Each table belongs to a project. Its name is used by people only: workflows choose it from a list. Its columns are what matters:

  • One table per kind of thing: one row is one customer, one ticket, one request. Avoid a table whose rows mean different things.
  • Keys are permanent: the key is the name workflows use ({{ ticket.row.subject }}). It cannot be changed later, and neither can the type. Choose them with care: email, amount, status.
  • Use the type that fits: Number for amounts and quantities, so they compare as numbers and can be summed. Email and Url check the value. Date or Datetime for times, so they sort and compare.
  • A status as a Select: with choices such as pending, approved, rejected, one per line. Only those values are accepted, so a typo in a workflow is an error instead of a silent new status.
  • Required for what every row must have. A workflow that forgets it fails with a clear message.
  • An external id: when rows come from another system, keep its id in a column (sku, order_no, message_id). It is what Insert or update matches on.

Every row also has, without a column for them: id (made by Rail22), created_at and updated_at. Conditions and sorting can use them too.

Example: a tickets table

LabelKeyTypeNotes
Message idmessage_idTextRequired. The email's id: a message is recorded once.
FromfromEmailRequired.
SubjectsubjectText
CustomercustomerObject, points to Data table: customersEmpty when the sender is not a known customer.
StatusstatusSelect: new, open, closedRequired.
Assigned toassigneeObject, points to User

Relations between tables

A column of type Object points to a row of another data table, to a user, or to a file. It holds the id of what it points to. In a workflow:

  • To set it, give the id: {{ customer.rows[0].id }} for a row found earlier, {{ form_user.id }} for the person who sent a form.
  • To follow it, use Get a row (by id) on the other table with Row id {{ ticket.row.customer }}.
  • To find the rows that point to something, query with the condition customer equals {{ customer.row.id }}.

Keep the details of a thing in one table and point to it from the others. A customer's email then changes in one place.

Reading rows

Query rows gives the rows that match its conditions. Each condition is a column, an operator and a value. The operators are those of If: equals, greater than, contains, is one of, is empty and the others. Values may be expressions. With no condition, every row matches.

SettingExample
Tabletickets
OperationQuery rows
Rows matchingAll conditions
Conditionsstatus is one of new, open
created_at less than {{ Date(Date.now() - 2 * 86400000).toISOString() }}
Sort bycreated_at, Ascending
Limit50
Result variablestale_tickets

This finds the tickets still new or open after two days, oldest first. The result:

{{ stale_tickets.count }}          the rows returned (at most the Limit)
{{ stale_tickets.total }}          all the rows that match
{{ stale_tickets.rows[0].subject }}
{{ stale_tickets.rows.map(t => t.subject).join(", ") }}

A query returns at most 1000 rows. For more, page through them with Skip, or narrow the conditions. total tells how many there are.

Get a row (by id) gives one row in row, or nothing when there is no such row: test it with an If, {{ customer.row }} is empty.

Writing rows

OperationUse it toResult
Insert a rowRecord something new.{ row }
Insert rows (a list)Load a whole list at once, e.g. {{ response.body.items }}: objects keyed by column. Up to 10,000 rows.{ inserted }
Insert or update (by a column)Keep a table in step with another system, or record something once.{ row, operation }: insert or update
Update a row (by id)Change one known row, e.g. its status.{ row }
Update rows (filter)Change every matching row.{ updated }
Delete a row (by id) / Delete rows (filter)Remove rows.{ deleted }
Get the columnsRead the table's design, e.g. for an AI step.{ columns }

The values are column / value rows. A value that is one expression alone keeps its type: {{ form.amount }} is stored as a number in a Number column. Values are checked against the columns: a required column left empty, a choice not in the list, or text in a Number column is an error. The step fails, or continues on its error output when On error says so, with the reason in <variable>.error.

Update only sets the columns you list. The others keep their values.

Patterns

Lookup

Find the data a run needs: the customer of an email address, the manager of a department. Query with one condition (email equals {{ mail.from }}), Limit 1, then use {{ customer.rows[0].name }}. An If on {{ customer.count }} equals 0 handles the unknown ones.

A small mapping table (a code and an address, a country and a manager) keeps such rules out of the workflow: people change the table, and the workflow stays the same.

Record once

Use Insert or update with Match by column set to the source's id. The first time a row is inserted, later times it is updated. {{ ticket.operation }} says which, so an If on it equals insert lets only new items continue, for example to send a notification once.

Work queue

One workflow adds rows with status pending. Another, on a Schedule, queries the pending ones (Limit 50, oldest first), handles each in a Loop, and updates its status to done or failed. The queue survives restarts, people can see it, and a failed row can be set back to pending by hand to try again.

Keeping a copy in step

Read the source's list, Insert or update each item by its id, and set a seen_at column to the run's time. Afterwards Delete rows (filter) seen_at less than that time removes what the source no longer has. See Example: product sync.

Log

Insert one row per run or per item with what happened: the time, the input, the result. Unlike the execution log, it is yours: it keeps the columns you chose, and people can filter, sort and export it.

People and tables

Tables are visible to the project's members, who can browse, filter, edit and import rows on the table's page. That makes a table a simple interface: a list of customers that the sales team keeps up to date, a queue that the support team watches. A row edited by hand is checked against the same column rules as one written by a workflow.

AI steps can work with tables too, when you allow their data table tools: list and query the tables, insert, update and delete rows. See AI steps.

Limits

  • A query returns at most 1000 rows. A Loop takes at most 1000 items.
  • Insert rows (a list) takes at most 10,000 rows at once.
  • Your plan may limit the number of tables and the rows in one table: a step that would go over fails with a message. The Usage page shows where you stand.

pages.title: Building an agent
pages.summary: An AI step that uses the integrations as tools: a GravityZone incident investigated and summarized, and the attacker's IP blocked on the FortiGate after a person approves.
pages.html:
An agent is an AI step with tools: it reads the situation, decides what to look up, calls the tools it needs, and writes up what it found. In Rail22 its tools can be the operations of your integrations (GravityZone, FortiGate, Veeam, vCenter, Proxmox, Hyper-V, Checkmk, Zabbix, Wazuh, Namecheap, Shopify, Nextcloud, Jira, HubSpot, Salesforce, GLPI, Intune, databases, email, Microsoft 365, Google), other workflows of the project, data tables and knowledge bases. This guide builds one that investigates a GravityZone incident, summarizes it, and blocks the attacker's address on the FortiGate once a person approves.

When to use an agent

Use fixed steps when you know the path: when a backup job fails, open a ticket. Use an agent when the next step depends on what is found: which endpoints are affected, whether the threat was blocked, which address it talks to. Let it read freely, and let a person approve what it changes.

The example: a GravityZone incident

GravityZone event (New incident)           gz
  → Investigate (Claude)                   reads GravityZone; asks to block an address on the FortiGate
      ↳ My tasks: "Approve: Block IPs 203.0.113.7, Blocked on FortiGate fw-hq"
  → Note on the incident                   GravityZone Incidents: Set the note
  → Tell the SOC team                      Send email

Before you start: a GravityZone credential and a FortiGate credential in the project, and on the FortiGate an address group (here Blocked) used by a deny policy.

1. The trigger

GravityZone event, Event types New incident and New extended incident, One run per event, variable gz.

2. The agent

An AI step, here Claude (Anthropic), named Investigate:

SettingValue
System promptYou are a SOC analyst. Investigate the GravityZone incident with your tools: get the incident, the endpoint's details, and whether other endpoints show the same threat. Take ids and addresses from the tools' results, never guess them. When an endpoint talks to an external address that the incident shows as malicious, block that address on the FortiGate (group Blocked), with a one-line reason. A person approves each block: if one is rejected, read why and say so in your summary. Be brief and factual.
PromptGravityZone reported this event: {{ gz }}
AnswerJSON, with the schema below.
Integrations…: Bitdefender GravityZoneThe credential; Operations: the read ones, ticked by default (List endpoints, Get endpoint details, List incidents, Get an incident, List quarantined items, …).
Integrations…: FortiGateThe credential; Operations: Addresses: List addresses and Addresses: Block IPs; Ask for approval: Write operations (the default): blocking waits for a person, listing does not.
Approvals…Approvers: the SOC role; Time limit: 4 hours (an address not approved by then is not blocked).
Rounds15: every round of tool calls is one call to the model.
On errorContinue on the error output, to tell the team the investigation did not finish.

The JSON schema makes the answer usable by the next steps:

{"type": "object",
 "properties": {
   "incidentId": {"type": "string"},
   "severity":   {"type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]},
   "endpoints":  {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
   "blocked":    {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "description": "addresses blocked on the FortiGate"},
   "summary":    {"type": "string", "description": "Markdown: what happened, evidence, actions, next steps"}
 },
 "required": ["incidentId", "severity", "endpoints", "blocked", "summary"],
 "additionalProperties": false}

3. The approval

When the agent calls fgt_addresses_block, the address is not blocked yet. The SOC team gets a task in My tasks:

Approve: Block IPs 203.0.113.7, Blocked on FortiGate fw-hq

Investigate (an AI step) asks to do this:
Block IPs 203.0.113.7, Blocked on FortiGate fw-hq
Why: Incident 42: malware on PC-ACCT-07 talks to 203.0.113.7
Tool: fgt_addresses_block (FortiGate Addresses: Block IPs (address + group))
- ips: 203.0.113.7
- group: Blocked

Block IPs 203.0.113.7, Blocked on FortiGate fw-hq:  Approve / Reject
Comment

The run waits; the server can restart meanwhile. Approve: the address is blocked and the agent goes on with the result. Reject with a comment, such as this is our CDN: nothing is blocked, and the agent reads rejected by Maria Lopez: this is our CDN and writes it in its summary. With no answer in 4 hours the block is refused.

4. After the agent

  1. GravityZone Incidents, operation Set the note, Incident {{ ai.json.incidentId }}, Note {{ ai.json.summary }}.
  2. Send email to the SOC team, subject Incident {{ ai.json.incidentId }}: {{ ai.json.severity }}, with the summary and the blocked addresses in a text block.

What a run looks like

The model sees tools such as gz_incidents_get (arguments incidentId, kind), gz_endpoints_details (endpointId), fgt_addresses_list and fgt_addresses_block (ips, group, and reason for the approver). The execution's log shows each call under the AI step, the wait, and the decision:

Claude (Anthropic): tool gz_incidents_get
GravityZone Incidents get: incident 6a1f… (183 ms)
Claude (Anthropic): tool gz_endpoints_details
GravityZone Endpoints details: endpoint PC-ACCT-07 (95 ms)
Claude (Anthropic): waiting for approval: Approve: Block IPs 203.0.113.7, Blocked on FortiGate fw-hq
…
FortiGate Addresses block: 1 IP blocked (group Blocked) (210 ms)
Claude (Anthropic): tool fgt_addresses_block (approved by Maria Lopez)
Claude (Anthropic): claude-opus-5-5, 5 round(s), 4 tool call(s), 21480 + 1710 tokens

ai.tool_calls lists the calls with their arguments, and for the block approval and by. A call with wrong arguments, or a step that failed, comes back to the model as an error: it usually corrects the call in the next round.

Choosing the tools

  • Start with the read operations, which are ticked by default. Add a write operation only when the task needs it, and keep Ask for approval on it.
  • Name the approvers (users or a role) and set a time limit, so that a request nobody sees does not wait forever.
  • Give the agent a credential of its own, with the rights its task needs, where the product allows it (a GravityZone API key with only the APIs it reads, a FortiGate API user limited to the addresses).
  • Fewer tools make better choices. Several agents, each with the tools of one area, can work together: a called workflow may have its own AI step, so a lead agent can ask a backup agent (Veeam tools) and use its outputs. At most 5 workflows are nested, and a workflow already in the chain cannot be started again.

Testing

  • Try the agent on a sample event while you build: a copy of the workflow that starts with a Manual Trigger and a Set step putting a real event (from an earlier run) in gz.
  • Reject the first approval with a comment, and check that the agent reports it.
  • Read the execution's agent trace: which tools were called, with which arguments, what came back, and who decided.
  • Change the prompt and use Run again to compare it on the same event. Write operations run again too, so try it on a test system or with approvals on.

See AI steps for every setting, and My tasks for the approver's side.

Before it goes to production

Save a few runs as test cases, so that a later change to the prompt, model or tools is checked before it is published. Set the step's Guardrails: a limit on tool calls, write calls and cost, and Lockdown after untrusted input if it reads mail, web pages or files and can also change things. Connect the error output, so a limit that stops the agent is handled. Check what it did under Agent actions in the audit log.

To let people talk to an agent instead of starting it on an event, see An IT helpdesk agent.

pages.title: An IT helpdesk agent
pages.summary: An agent people talk to: it asks Checkmk and Veeam for the status, remembers who it talks to, and opens a ticket after asking.
pages.html:
This guide builds an agent colleagues talk to when something does not work. It checks Checkmk and Veeam for what is known, remembers what it learns about each person, and opens a ticket when the person agrees. It builds on Building an agent.

Chat                     message, conversation, user
  → Helpdesk (Claude)    reads Checkmk and Veeam; remember, recall; runs Open a ticket
  → Answer               Reply to chat: {{ ai.text }}

Before you start: a Checkmk credential and a Veeam credential in the project, and an AI credential.

1. The tickets and the memory

Under Data Tables, make two tables:

  • Tickets, with text columns title, details and requester;
  • Helpdesk memory, with text columns fact and scope.

2. Opening a ticket: a workflow of its own

A workflow does the same thing every time: a good place for what must not vary. Make a workflow Open a ticket:

Called by a workflow     inputs: title, details, requester; outputs: ticket
  → Data Table           Insert in Tickets
  → Set                  ticket = {{ table.row.id }}

In Called by a workflow, set Description for agents: Opens a helpdesk ticket. Use it only after the person has agreed. Publish it. To use your real ticket system, replace the Data Table step with an HTTP Request.

3. The agent

Make a workflow Helpdesk that starts with a Chat trigger. Name the step IT helpdesk: that is the name people see. Set the greeting to Hello, what is not working?, and leave Users and Roles empty for every member of the project, Participants included.

Add an AI step:

SettingValue
System promptYou are the IT helpdesk of our company. You talk to {{ user.name }}. First find out what is not working. Check Checkmk for problems on the machines concerned, and Veeam when it is about backups or restores. Say what you found, in plain words. If it looks like a known problem, say so. If it needs a person, offer to open a ticket, and open it only after they agree: give it a title and everything you found. Remember lasting facts about the person, such as which site or machine they use; never passwords.
Prompt{{ message }}
Trusted variablesuser: their name in the system prompt comes from their account.
IntegrationsCheckmk: its credential, and cmk_status_problems, cmk_status_host, cmk_status_services. Veeam: its credential, and veeam_jobs_states, veeam_sessions_list, veeam_backups_latest. Only tools that read: these ask for no approval.
WorkflowsOpen a ticket.
ConversationContinue the conversation on. The other settings can stay.
Long-term memoryRemember in: A data table, Helpdesk memory. Whose memories: Each person's own.
GuardrailsMost tool calls per run: 15. Cost limit per run: what a question is worth to you.

Then add Reply to chat, with the answer {{ ai.text }} as Markdown. Connect them, and publish.

4. Talk to it

Under Agents, open IT helpdesk and write The file server is slow. The agent looks up the host and answers. Then write and last night's backup?: it knows you still mean the file server, because the earlier turns go to the model. When you agree to a ticket, it runs Open a ticket, and the new row is in Tickets.

Under Executions, each message is a run. Its agent trace shows the tools called, what came back, and how many earlier turns the step was given.

5. Buttons for the ticket

To make agreeing a press of a button, add one to Reply to chat, for example with the label Yes, open a ticket and the value Yes, please open a ticket. To show it only when the agent offers one, have the AI step answer JSON, such as { "text": "...", "options": [ "Yes, open a ticket", "No, thanks" ] }, then use {{ ai.json.text }} as the answer and {{ ai.json.options }} in More buttons from.

Before people use it

  • What can it change? Here, only tickets. Before you give it a tool that changes something, such as acknowledging a problem or starting a backup job, keep Ask for approval on: colleagues should not be able to talk an agent into it. By default the person asking cannot approve it themselves.
  • Who reads this? People tell helpdesks things. The account's owners can read conversations, and whoever can open the workflow sees its runs. Say so to your colleagues. See Agents.
  • How long is it kept? By the account's log retention, and Helpdesk memory until someone deletes it.
  • Other ways in: Email (inbound) with Keep conversations for a helpdesk address, and Teams message for a chat. Each needs a workflow of its own, with the same steps: a workflow has one trigger. To keep them the same, put the agent in a workflow that starts with Called by a workflow.

pages.title: Examples
pages.summary: Complete workflows step by step: expense approval, emails to tickets, product sync.
pages.html:
These examples show complete workflows, step by step, with the settings that matter. Each one starts with the sketch, then the tables it needs, then the steps. Build them in a test project and adapt them.

ExampleShows
Expense approvalA Form, a record with a status, a Human task, a decision, emails.
Emails to ticketsA Schedule, reading a mailbox, a Loop, a lookup, recording each email once, a relation between tables.
Product syncCalling an API, keeping a table in step with it, removing what is gone, safe ordering.

The ideas behind them are in Modeling a workflow and Using data tables.

pages.title: Expense approval
pages.summary: A Form, a record with a status, a Human task for the manager, the decision recorded and emailed.
pages.html:
An employee asks for an expense to be approved. A manager approves or rejects it, the employee is told, and every request is recorded with its decision.

The sketch

Form (amount, reason)
  → Record request         Data Table: insert, status pending
  → Manager decides        Human task: approved / rejected, comment
  → Record decision        Data Table: update the row
  → Approved?              If
      true  → Email "approved"
      false → Email "rejected"

The table

Create a data table expenses:

LabelKeyTypeRequired
EmployeeemployeeObject, points to UserYes
AmountamountNumberYes
ReasonreasonTextareaYes
StatusstatusSelect: pending, approved, rejectedYes
Decided bydecided_byObject, points to User
CommentcommentTextarea

The steps

1. Form trigger

Who can fill it in: Project members, so that form_user tells who asked. Fields: Amount (number, key amount, required) and Reason (long text, key reason, required). Answers variable: form.

2. Data Table: Record request

SettingValue
Table / Operationexpenses / Insert a row
Valuesemployee = {{ form_user.id }}
amount = {{ form.amount }}
reason = {{ form.reason }}
status = pending
Result variableexpense

The request is recorded before the run waits for the manager. The table shows it as pending even if nobody answers.

3. Human task: Manager decides

SettingValue
TaskApprove {{ form.amount }} EUR for {{ form_user.name }}
InstructionsReason: {{ form.reason }}
Assigned rolesManagers
FormDecision (choice, key decision, required, choices approved and rejected), Comment (long text, key comment)
Time limitDays, after 3
Answers variabletask

The choices are the same as those of the status column, so the answer can be stored as it is. With the time limit, connect the timeout output to an email that reminds the managers, or to a Data Table update that sets the status to rejected with the comment No answer in time.

4. Data Table: Record decision

SettingValue
Table / Operationexpenses / Update a row (by id)
Row id{{ expense.row.id }}
Valuesstatus = {{ task.decision }}
decided_by = {{ task_user.id }}
comment = {{ task.comment }}
Result variableexpense

5. If: Approved?

{{ task.decision }} equals approved.

6. Send email (on each side)

To {{ form_user.email }}. On true: subject Your expense of {{ form.amount }} EUR is approved. On false: subject Your expense of {{ form.amount }} EUR was rejected, with {{ task_user.name }} and {{ task.comment }} in the message.

Variations

  • Two levels: a second If after the form, {{ form.amount }} greater than 1000, adds a Human task for the finance team before the manager's. A Merge brings both paths back to Record decision.
  • A report: a second workflow on a Schedule queries expenses with status equals pending every morning and emails the list to the managers.

pages.title: Emails to tickets
pages.summary: New emails of a mailbox become tickets, linked to known customers, recorded once.
pages.html:
Every few minutes, new emails in a support mailbox become tickets. A sender who is a known customer is linked to their customer row. An email is recorded only once, even when it is read again, and the team is told about each new ticket.

The sketch

Schedule (every 5 minutes)
  → Read emails            new messages, to mails
  → Loop over mails
      → Find customer      Data Table: query customers by email
      → Record ticket      Data Table: insert or update by message_id
      → New?               If ticket.operation equals insert
          true → Notify support (email)

The tables

customers: at least name (Text) and email (Email, required). Fill it by hand or import a CSV.

tickets: as in Using data tables: message_id (Text, required), from (Email, required), subject (Text), customer (Object, points to Data table: customers), status (Select: new, open, closed, required).

The steps

1. Schedule trigger

Every 5 minutes.

2. Read emails

The support mailbox's credential, folder INBOX, Read: New messages, Messages variable mails. The first run only notes where the folder ends. The next runs read what arrived since.

3. Loop

List {{ mails }}, item variable mail, On error in a pass: Skip the item and continue, so one bad email does not stop the others. With no new email the list is empty and the loop does nothing.

4. Data Table: Find customer (inside the loop)

SettingValue
Table / Operationcustomers / Query rows
Conditionsemail equals {{ mail.from }}
Limit1
Result variablecustomer

5. Data Table: Record ticket

SettingValue
Table / Operationtickets / Insert or update (by a column)
Match by columnmessage_id
Valuesmessage_id = {{ mail.message_id }}
from = {{ mail.from }}
subject = {{ mail.subject }}
customer = {{ customer.rows[0]?.id }}
status = new
Result variableticket

?. gives nothing instead of an error when no customer was found, and the ticket is recorded without one. The Match by column makes the step safe to repeat: an email read a second time updates its ticket instead of adding another.

Note: an update sets every value listed, so a ticket already set to open would go back to new if its email is read again. When that matters, query tickets by message_id first and continue only when count is 0, with Insert a row.

6. If: New?

{{ ticket.operation }} equals insert. Connect only the true output.

7. Send email: Notify support

To {{ vars.support_email }} (a project variable), subject New ticket: {{ mail.subject }}, and in the message From {{ customer.rows[0]?.name ?? mail.from }}.

Variations

  • Sort with AI: an AI step before Record ticket picks a category from the subject and text, and a Switch on it assigns the ticket to a team.
  • Escalate: a second workflow, every hour, queries the tickets still new created more than four hours ago and emails the team lead.

pages.title: Product sync
pages.summary: A nightly copy of an API's product list in a data table: add, update, remove what is gone.
pages.html:
Every night, the product list of an online shop's API is copied into a data table that other workflows look up. New products are added, changed ones are updated, and products the shop no longer has are removed.

The sketch

Schedule (daily, 02:00)
  → Get products           HTTP Request: GET /products
  → Loop over the products
      → Save product       Data Table: insert or update by sku, seen_at = this run
  → Remove the others      Data Table: delete rows seen_at before this run

The table

products: sku (Text, required), name (Text), price (Number), stock (Number), seen_at (Datetime, required).

seen_at is the trick: each run stamps every product it receives with its own time. A product with an older stamp was not in this run's list.

The steps

1. Schedule trigger

Daily at 02:00. The run's time is in {{ schedule_time }}.

2. HTTP Request: Get products

GET {{ vars.shop_api }}/products, with the shop's API key credential. Response variable response. On error: Fail the step.

Failing here is deliberate: when the API does not answer, the run stops before the delete step. Otherwise an empty answer would remove every product.

3. Loop

List {{ response.body.items }}, item variable product.

4. Data Table: Save product (inside the loop)

SettingValue
Table / Operationproducts / Insert or update (by a column)
Match by columnsku
Valuessku = {{ product.sku }}
name = {{ product.title }}
price = {{ product.price }}
stock = {{ product.stock }}
seen_at = {{ schedule_time }}
Result variablesaved

The API's field names (title) and the table's keys (name) need not be the same: the values map one to the other.

5. Data Table: Remove the others (after the loop)

SettingValue
Table / Operationproducts / Delete rows (filter)
Conditionsseen_at less than {{ schedule_time }}
Result variableremoved

{{ removed.deleted }} tells how many went. A Send email after it can report {{ response.body.items.length }} products, {{ removed.deleted }} removed.

Things to watch

  • Use a column for the run's time, not updated_at: a row whose values did not change is not saved again, so its updated_at stays old.
  • Large lists: a Loop takes at most 1000 items. For more, page through the API (a query parameter such as page) in several requests, or, for a first load into an empty table, use Insert rows (a list) with {{ response.body.items }} when the items' fields match the column keys.
  • A bad item: with On error in a pass set to Skip, a product the table refuses (no sku, a price that is not a number) is listed in loop.errors and the others are saved. Its row is not stamped, so the delete step removes it: decide whether that is what you want, or stop the run instead.
  • Testing: press Run in the designer. It runs once now, as a scheduled run of the current minute, so schedule_time is set. Try it first on a copy of the table, or with a Limit on the API, before it deletes anything that matters.

pages.title: Overview
pages.summary: The project's dashboard: how its workflows run, what failed, what is running and waiting.
pages.html:
The Overview, at the top of the sidebar, is the current project's dashboard. It shows how the project's workflows run.

Period

Choose 24h, 7d, 30d or 90d at the top. Everything below follows the period, and each figure is compared with the period before. Your browser remembers the choice.

What it shows

  • Figures: the executions, the success rate, the median run time, what is running now and what is waiting (sleeping runs), and the open tasks.
  • Executions over time: completed and failed runs, per hour or per day.
  • Executions by trigger: how runs were started: schedule, webhook, form, file upload, email, manual.
  • Run time by workflow: the median run time of each workflow, up to its slowest runs (95th percentile).
  • Workflows: a sortable table of the workflows, with their last run and a small chart of their runs.
  • Problems: the steps that fail most, and work that seems stuck. A run still going after 15 minutes has a Kill button (if you may edit its workflow). Killing stops the run, and it shows as Cancelled. It stops at once.
  • Recent executions: the latest runs.

Click Refresh to update the figures. To see one run in detail, open its workflow's Executions panel.

pages.title: Projects and members
pages.summary: Creating projects, switching between them, managing who is a member, and moving work to another server.
pages.html:
A project holds related work: workflows, credentials and variables, data tables and files. Only its members see what is inside.

Your personal project

Every user has a project called Personal, created the first time they sign in. Only they are a member of it, which makes it a good place to try things.

Switching projects

The current project's name is at the top of the sidebar. Click it to switch to another project you belong to. The sidebar then shows that project's workflows, credentials, tables and files.

Creating a project

Click + at the top of the sidebar and choose New project. You become its owner. Your role must allow creating projects.

Project settings

Click the gear icon at the top of the sidebar to open the current project's settings. It has these tabs:

  • General: the project's icon and name.
  • Members: who is in the project, and with which role.
  • Export / import: move workflows, credentials and data tables to another Rail22 server. Shown to roles that may export and import (Owner by default).

Members

  • Add a member: choose a user of the account and a role.
  • Invite by email: an address that is already a user of the account is added at once. Any other address receives a link to join. Pending invitations are listed with Resend and Cancel.
  • Change a role: choose another role in the member's row. The change is saved right away.
  • Remove: takes the user out of the project. The last member with the Owner role cannot be removed or changed.

A member's role in the project decides what they may do in it, for example build workflows (Member) or only fill in forms and complete tasks (Participant). See Roles and permissions.

A personal project has no other members.

Moving work to another server

To move work between Rail22 servers, for example from development to pre-production, export it to a file on one server and import that file into a project on the other.

Export

  • Tick the workflows, credentials and variables, and data tables to include. Also the credentials and data tables the chosen workflows use adds what their steps need.
  • Tick with rows on a data table to include its data. Otherwise only its columns are exported.
  • Workflows are exported as their drafts: the steps as last saved in the designer.
  • Passphrase: with one, the file is encrypted and includes the credentials' secrets (passwords, keys, tokens). Without one, the file has no secrets, and you enter them again after the import. Each server encrypts secrets with its own key, so the two servers do not need the same APP_SECRET.

Import

Choose the file and enter its passphrase, if it has one. The next page lists everything in the file. Items are matched to this project's by name, and for each one you choose what to do:

ItemNot in the projectAlready in the project
Data tableCreateUpdate its columns and keep its rows (default); update its columns and replace its rows (if the file has rows); create a copy; skip
CredentialCreateSkip and keep this server's (default); replace it; create a copy
WorkflowCreateReplace its draft (default); create a copy; skip

Nothing changes until you click Import. Then:

  • Steps are pointed at this server's credentials and data tables: the imported ones, or the ones of the same name already in the project. The import page warns about anything the steps use that is in neither the file nor the project.
  • Imported workflows are drafts. Check them in the designer, then publish them. A replaced workflow that was published keeps running its live version until you publish the new draft.
  • Webhook, form and email triggers keep their token, so on the new server their URL differs only in the host name. A replaced workflow keeps the URLs it already had. If another workflow on the server already uses a token, the step gets a new one.
  • Columns that exist on both sides are updated. Columns only on this server are kept, with their data.
  • OAuth credentials need this server's redirect URI added to the app at the provider. Then use Connect again.

Files, executions, published versions and user assignments (for example a task's assignee) are not exported. Each export and import is recorded in the audit log.

pages.title: Forms
pages.summary: The list of the forms people can fill in, and how forms are shared.
pages.html:
Forms, in the sidebar, lists the forms of the account's published workflows that you can open: one per Form trigger. Click one to fill it in. Sending it starts its workflow.

When the list is empty, no published workflow has a Form trigger yet. Add one to a workflow and publish it.

Sharing a form

Each form has its own address, shown in the Form trigger's settings. What happens when someone opens it depends on the trigger's Who can fill it in:

  • Project members (logged in): visitors are asked to sign in, then come back to the form.
  • Anyone with the link: no sign-in, so customers or partners can fill it in.

After sending, the visitor sees the trigger's Message after sending.

pages.title: Agents
pages.summary: Talk to the agents of your projects; who can read the conversations, how long they are kept.
pages.html:
Agents, in the sidebar, lists the agents you may talk to: the published workflows of the account that start with a Chat trigger and allow you. You need no other permission: Participants have the same page.

Click an agent to open its chat. Write a message and press Enter (Shift+Enter for a new line); when an answer has buttons, you can press one or type. Your conversations with it are listed beside it: open one to go on, or start a new one. The bin deletes the one that is open.

The agent may have to wait for someone to approve what it wants to do, and the page says so. See My tasks.

Who can read the conversations

  • You read and delete your own.
  • The account's owners read and delete every conversation: All conversations, at the top of the Agents page. Each shows the messages, the tools used on each turn and the older turns' summary. Deleting one is recorded in the audit log.
  • Whoever can open the workflow sees what a run holds, the message and the earlier turns included, in its Executions.

How long they are kept

By the account's log retention (Account settings): messages, summaries and the runs that hold their text go when they are older than that, and a conversation with them. With no limit set, they stay until they are deleted. Deleting a conversation takes its messages at once; its runs follow by the same retention. Facts an agent saved with remember are not part of this: they stay in their table or knowledge base.

pages.title: My tasks
pages.summary: The tasks assigned to you by workflows and agents, and how to complete or approve them.
pages.html:
My tasks, in the sidebar, lists the open tasks assigned to you by Human task steps, and the actions of AI agents waiting for your approval. A badge shows how many there are. Tasks come from all the account's projects you belong to.

Completing a task

  1. Click a task to open it. You see its instructions and its form.
  2. Fill in the form and press the button, for example Complete or Approve.
  3. The workflow that was waiting continues with your answers.

A task assigned to a role or to several people can be completed by any of them. Once someone has completed it, it leaves everyone's list. If a task reaches its time limit first, it expires and can no longer be completed. Opening it then says "This task is no longer open."

Approving an agent's action
