pages.title: SAP Cloud Integration (SAP plugin)
pages.summary: The SAP plugin's first integration: call iFlows, monitor messages and artifacts, deploy, and start workflows when a message fails on SAP Cloud Integration.
pages.html:
The SAP plugin connects Rail22 to SAP products. Its first integration is SAP Cloud Integration (CPI, part of SAP Integration Suite on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry; Neo with Basic sign-in). Workflows can call an iFlow, read message processing logs and deployed artifacts, deploy or undeploy an integration flow, make any call of the Cloud Integration OData API, and start when a message fails. The plugin is made so that SAP Business One and S/4HANA can be added to it later, as further credentials and steps.

Its steps are in the SAP group of the step list, and its credentials in the SAP group. They are available to every account of an installation that has the plugin.

The steps

StepWhat it doesCredential
SAP CPI Call an iFlowSends a request to an iFlow: status, headers, the answer, the message processing log id.SAP Cloud Integration (iFlows)
SAP CPI MonitoringMessage processing logs (a list, one with its error, its attachments), deployed artifacts, packages, any read of the API.SAP Cloud Integration (API)
SAP CPI ManageDeploys or undeploys an integration flow; any call of the API.SAP Cloud Integration (API)
SAP CPI failed message (trigger)Starts the workflow when a message fails (optionally also in Retry or escalated).SAP Cloud Integration (API)

Calls from Cloud Integration to Rail22 use the core's Webhook trigger: see Calls from Cloud Integration.

Installing

On a hosted installation, the plugin is there when the installation offers it. On a self-hosted one, clone it into the app's plugins folder and add its entry to plugins.json, next to app.env (see Plugins overview):

git clone <the plugin's repository> app/plugins/SAP
# add to plugins.json:  "SAP": { "enabled": true }

Restart PHP-FPM and the daemon. Update it with git pull in app/plugins/SAP, along with Rail22's own update. The plugin is licensed under the GNU AGPL v3, as Rail22.

Setting up the service keys

Cloud Integration gives two kinds of access, each from a service instance of the Process Integration Runtime service with its own plan, and Rail22 has a credential for each. In the SAP BTP cockpit, in the subaccount of your Integration Suite:

  1. Go to Services > Service Marketplace and choose Process Integration Runtime (the tile appears once Cloud Integration's runtime and a space exist), then Create.
  2. For calling iFlows: plan integration-flow, runtime environment Cloud Foundry, a space. Under Roles keep ESBMessaging.send (or the custom role your iFlows' sender adapters ask for), grant type Client Credentials.
  3. For monitoring and management: plan api, with the roles the workflows need, such as MonitoringDataRead (message processing logs), WorkspacePackagesRead (packages) and WorkspaceArtifactsDeploy (deploy, undeploy); grant type Client Credentials.
  4. In Instances and Subscriptions, choose each instance and Create Service Key. Key type ClientId/Secret, or Certificate (SAP issues a client certificate and key).
  5. Open the key and copy it whole. In Rail22, under Credentials & variables, create an SAP Cloud Integration (iFlows) credential with the integration-flow key, and an SAP Cloud Integration (API) credential with the api key. Paste the key into Service key (JSON): it fills the fields and is not kept.

The iFlows key's url is the runtime's address (it usually contains -rt); the iFlows are at that address followed by /http/ and their address. The api key's url is the tenant's address; the API is at /api/v1 after it. The integration-flow plan's tokens last an hour by default, the api plan's twelve hours: Rail22 keeps a token while it runs and asks for a new one shortly before it expires, or once when the tenant answers 401.

Neo: there are no service keys. Choose Sign-in: Basic and give the address of the tenant (its runtime for iFlows, its management node for the API), a user and its password.

The credentials

Both credentials have the same fields. Test on an iFlows credential signs in and says when the token expires (or until when the certificate is valid); with Test iFlow it also calls that iFlow (GET) and shows its status. Test on an API credential signs in and lists the deployed artifacts it can read.

SettingDescription
Service key (JSON)Paste the whole service key (SAP BTP cockpit > Instances and Subscriptions > the instance > its key): it fills the fields below and is not kept.
Sign-inChoices: OAuth: client id and secret; Client certificate (key type Certificate); Basic: user and password (Neo). Default: OAuth: client id and secret. Required.
URLThe service key's url: the runtime's address (iFlows), or the tenant's (API).
Token URLThe service key's tokenurl.
Client id / userThe service key's clientid; Basic: the user.
Client secret / passwordThe service key's clientsecret; Basic: the password. Stored encrypted.
Client certificateThe service key's certificate: -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- ... (PEM, with its chain).
Private keyThe service key's key: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- ... (PEM, unencrypted). Stored encrypted.
Trusted CA certificatesOnly when the server's certificate is issued by a CA the system does not trust (e.g. a corporate proxy): PEM; the system's CAs stay trusted.
Test iFlow(iFlows credential only) An iFlow's address after /http/ that Test calls (GET).

The server's certificate is always checked. Rail22 connects only to public internet addresses unless the account allows private network addresses (Account settings).

What the steps share

  • Lists give { items, count, total, truncated }, at most At most (items). The API answers in pages; the steps follow them until At most.
  • Writes to the API (deploy, undeploy, Call the API with POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE) first fetch a CSRF token, as the API requires; a token that has expired is fetched again once. An iFlow whose sender adapter is CSRF protected is handled the same way.
  • Busy: an answer 429 or 503 is waited for once (its Retry-After, at most 30 seconds).
  • Errors: Cloud Integration's own message and code, such as SAP Cloud Integration: Integration design time artifact not found (Not Found). With On error set to continue, the step goes on through its error output.
  • Times are given as ISO 8601 in UTC, such as 2026-11-11T08:30:00.000Z.
  • No secret (client secret, token, private key) is written to the logs or to the variables.

AI steps

An AI step can use the Monitoring and Manage steps as tools, in its Integrations… section, with an SAP Cloud Integration (API) credential. Monitoring only reads; Manage changes the tenant: its tools are not offered by default and ask for approval when approvals are on.

IntegrationTool namesOperationsCredential
SAP Cloud Integrationcpi_…, e.g. cpi_monitor_logs, cpi_manage_deploy11 (8 read)SAP Cloud Integration (API)

Call an iFlow is not offered as a tool. An iFlow usually writes into SAP systems, and SAP's API Policy restricts (semi-)autonomous AI systems that plan and run SAP API calls. A workflow that calls an iFlow can still be offered to an AI step by its owner, as a workflow tool (wf_…), where the workflow, not the model, decides what is sent.

SAP's API Policy and licensing

Note: SAP API Policy v.4.2026 (April 2026), section 2.2.2, prohibits API use for "interaction or integration with (semi-)autonomous or generative AI systems that plan, select, or execute sequences of API calls", except through SAP-endorsed architectures and pathways. The Cloud Integration OData API is itself an SAP API: before you give the Monitoring or Manage tools to an AI step, check with your SAP contact that this use is allowed for your contract. Workflows that run fixed steps, without a model choosing the calls, are ordinary integrations.

Documents that a workflow creates in an SAP ERP system through an iFlow (sales orders, invoices, ...) can count as digital access (indirect use) under your SAP license. Rail22 does not count or report them: check with your SAP account team how such documents are licensed for you.

Not confirmed

These parts follow SAP's documentation (help.sap.com, the Process Integration Runtime and the Cloud Integration OData API), but were checked only against a test tenant made from it, not yet against a real one:

  • That an iFlow's answer carries the SAP_MessageProcessingLogID header. SAP documents it as a header of the message inside the iFlow, and says the HTTPS sender adapter returns the message's headers; the step also reads the id an error text names.
  • The form of a pasted service key: it is read whether its fields are at the top or under oauth.
  • The content of a message's attachments (MessageProcessingLogAttachments('<id>')/$value), and the values of the deploy task's status (BuildAndDeployStatus: SUCCESS, FAIL); the task id as the deploy answer's text.
  • That messages in Retry have an end time the trigger can filter on, and that the API reads the times of a filter as UTC.
  • The addresses on Neo.

pages.title: SAP CPI Call an iFlow
pages.summary: Sends a request to an iFlow deployed on SAP Cloud Integration and gives its answer and message processing log id.
pages.html:
The SAP CPI Call an iFlow step sends a request to an iFlow deployed on your Cloud Integration tenant: to the address of its HTTPS sender adapter, <runtime url>/http/<address>. It uses an SAP Cloud Integration (iFlows) credential (a service key of plan integration-flow, see SAP Cloud Integration).

Give the iFlow's address after /http/ (as set in its sender adapter, such as orders/create), the method, and the body: text, JSON, XML, or a project file ({{ file }} of another step). The content type follows the body unless you set one. Query parameters reach the iFlow as headers; your own headers must be in the iFlow's Allowed Headers.

The answer is parsed when it is JSON or XML (attributes as @name, a repeated element as a list, text beside elements as #text); other text stays text; a binary answer (a PDF, an image) is saved to the project's Files and given as file.

A status outside 200–299 is an error, with Cloud Integration's text and the message id, unless Treat any status as success is on: then the step goes on and you check {{ iflow.status }}. The messageId is the message processing log id: a later SAP CPI Monitoring step can read that message (Get a message processing log).

Note: this step is not offered to AI steps as a tool (see SAP Cloud Integration, AI steps).

Settings

SettingDescription
SAP Cloud Integration (iFlows) credentialA credential of the project. Required.
MethodChoices: POST; GET; PUT; PATCH; DELETE. Default: POST.
iFlow addressThe address of its HTTPS sender adapter, after /http/ (e.g. orders/create). Required.
QueryA JSON object of query parameters (the iFlow gets them as headers); empty: none.
HeadersName: value, one per line (or a JSON object); the iFlow must allow them (Allowed Headers).
BodyChoices: None; Text; JSON; XML; A project file. Default: JSON.
Content typeEmpty: from the body (application/json, application/xml, text/plain, the file's).
ContentText, JSON or XML (with {{ }}); JSON: a value of another step is sent as JSON.
FileA project file: {{ file }} of another step, or its id.
Treat any status as successOff: a status outside 200-299 is an error (On error) with Cloud Integration's text. Default: off.
Timeout (s)Default: 60. Required.
Result variableWhat the operation gives. Default: iflow. Required.
On errorSAP's errors, or no connection. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the `error` output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription
iflowobject{ status, ok, headers, contentType, body, messageId, file }
iflow.statusnumberthe HTTP status
iflow.okbooleana status 200-299
iflow.headersobjectlower-case name => value
iflow.contentTypestring
iflow.bodyanyJSON or XML parsed when possible, else the text; null when saved as a file
iflow.messageIdstringthe message processing log id (null when the answer has none)
iflow.fileobject{ id, filename, size, contentType } of a binary answer (null otherwise)

pages.title: SAP CPI Monitoring
pages.summary: Reads SAP Cloud Integration: message processing logs and their errors and attachments, deployed artifacts, packages.
pages.html:
The SAP CPI Monitoring step reads your Cloud Integration tenant through its OData API, with an SAP Cloud Integration (API) credential whose key has the roles to read it (such as MonitoringDataRead). It changes nothing.

List message processing logs filters by status (Failed by default), iFlow names, the time the messages ended (an ISO time such as 2026-11-01T08:00:00Z, or a relative one such as -2 hours), correlation id or application message id; newest first. Get a message processing log takes a message id, such as {{ iflow.messageId }} of Call an iFlow or {{ cpi.messageGuid }} of the failed message trigger, and adds its error text.

Operations

OperationCallsResult
List message processing logsGET MessageProcessingLogs ($filter, $orderby LogEnd desc)A list of messages: messageGuid, iflow, iflowId, status, customStatus, logStart, logEnd, correlationId, applicationMessageId, applicationMessageType, sender, receiver, logLevel, transactionId, link
Get a message processing logGET MessageProcessingLogs('<id>') and its ErrorInformationThe message, with errorText
List a message's attachmentsGET MessageProcessingLogs('<id>')/AttachmentsA list: id, name, contentType, size, timeStamp, file (with Save their content)
List deployed artifactsGET IntegrationRuntimeArtifactsA list: id, name, version, type, status, deployedBy, deployedOn
Get a deployed artifactGET IntegrationRuntimeArtifacts('<id>') and its ErrorInformationThe artifact, with errorText when it is in error
List integration packagesGET IntegrationPackagesA list: id, name, version, shortText, vendor, mode, createdBy, modifiedBy, modifiedAt
List a package's integration flowsGET IntegrationPackages('<id>')/IntegrationDesigntimeArtifactsA list: id, name, version, packageId, description
Call the API (read)GET of any resource after /api/v1/The decoded answer (OData's d)

Settings

SettingDescription
SAP Cloud Integration (API) credentialA credential of the project. Required.
OperationChoices: List message processing logs; Get a message processing log; List a message's attachments; List deployed artifacts; Get a deployed artifact; List integration packages; List a package's integration flows; Call the API (read). Default: List message processing logs. Required.
StatusChoices: Any status; Failed; Retry; Escalated; Completed; Processing; Cancelled; Discarded; Abandoned. Default: Failed. (For: List message processing logs.)
iFlowsTheir names, separated by commas; empty: all. (For: List message processing logs.)
Ended fromA time (2026-11-01T08:00:00Z) or a relative one (-1 hour); empty: no limit. (For: List message processing logs.)
Ended untilEmpty: now. (For: List message processing logs.)
Correlation id(For: List message processing logs.)
Application message id(For: List message processing logs.)
MessageIts message processing log id, e.g. {{ iflow.messageId }} or {{ cpi.messageGuid }}. (Required for: Get a message processing log, List a message's attachments.)
Save their contentEach attachment saved to the project's Files. Default: off. (For: List a message's attachments.)
StatusChoices: Any status; Started; Starting; Error; Stopping. Default: Any status. (For: List deployed artifacts.)
ArtifactIts id (e.g. the iFlow's id). (Required for: Get a deployed artifact.)
PackageIts id. (Required for: List a package's integration flows.)
PathA resource of the API, after /api/v1/ (e.g. MessageProcessingLogs, IntegrationRuntimeArtifacts('MyFlow')). (Required for: Call the API (read).)
QueryA JSON object of the query's options, e.g. {"$filter": "Status eq 'FAILED'", "$top": 10}; empty: none. (For: Call the API (read).)
At most (items)Of a list: more are left out (truncated). Default: 1000. Required. (For: List message processing logs, List a message's attachments, List deployed artifacts, List integration packages, List a package's integration flows.)
Timeout (s)Default: 60. Required.
Result variableA list: { items, count, total, truncated }; otherwise what the operation gives. Default: cpi. Required.
On errorSAP's errors, or no connection. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the `error` output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

pages.title: SAP CPI Manage
pages.summary: Changes SAP Cloud Integration: deploys and undeploys integration flows, or makes any call of its OData API.
pages.html:
The SAP CPI Manage step changes your Cloud Integration tenant through its OData API, with an SAP Cloud Integration (API) credential whose key has the roles for it (such as WorkspaceArtifactsDeploy).

Deploy an integration flow deploys a design-time integration flow by its id and version (active: the latest saved). With Wait until deployed (on by default), the step reads the build and deploy status every 3 seconds until it is done; a failed build is an error. Undeploy an artifact removes a deployed artifact from the runtime. Call the API makes any call: a method, a resource after /api/v1/, a query (a JSON object, such as {"$filter": "Status eq 'ERROR'"}) and a JSON body.

Each write carries a CSRF token, fetched first as the API requires.

Operations

OperationCallsResult
Deploy an integration flowPOST DeployIntegrationDesigntimeArtifact?Id='<id>'&Version='<version>', then BuildAndDeployStatus(TaskId=…){ id, version, taskId, status }
Undeploy an artifactDELETE IntegrationRuntimeArtifacts('<id>'){ id, undeployed }
Call the APIAny method on a resource after /api/v1/The decoded answer

Settings

SettingDescription
SAP Cloud Integration (API) credentialA credential of the project. Required.
OperationChoices: Deploy an integration flow; Undeploy an artifact; Call the API. Default: Deploy an integration flow. Required.
ArtifactIts id (the integration flow's id). (Required for: Deploy an integration flow, Undeploy an artifact.)
VersionIts version, or active (the latest saved). Default: active. (For: Deploy an integration flow.)
Wait until deployedThe build and deploy status read until it is done (within the timeout). Default: on. (For: Deploy an integration flow.)
MethodChoices: GET; POST; PUT; PATCH; DELETE. Default: GET. (For: Call the API.)
PathA resource of the API, after /api/v1/ (e.g. IntegrationRuntimeArtifacts('MyFlow')). (Required for: Call the API.)
QueryA JSON object of the query's options, e.g. {"$filter": "Status eq 'FAILED'", "$top": 10}; empty: none. (For: Call the API.)
BodyA JSON object (or list) sent as the body; empty: none. (For: Call the API.)
Timeout (s)Default: 60. Required.
Result variableWhat the operation gives. Default: cpi. Required.
On errorSAP's errors, or no connection. Choices: Fail the step; Continue on the `error` output. Default: Fail the step. Required.

pages.title: SAP CPI failed message
pages.summary: A trigger: starts the workflow when a message fails on SAP Cloud Integration.
pages.html:
The SAP CPI failed message trigger starts the workflow when a message fails on your Cloud Integration tenant. It checks on its schedule (every 5 minutes by default) through an SAP Cloud Integration (API) credential (role MonitoringDataRead): it reads the message processing logs with status Failed (and, when chosen, Retry and Escalated) of all iFlows or of those named, that ended since the last check.

  • Each message starts one run. The first check only notes the messages already there: runs start with the next failure.
  • A log can be written a little after the message ended. Each check therefore also reads Look-back minutes before the last check (2 by default); a message read twice still starts one run.
  • One run per message gives the message with its error text (cut to 4000 characters); One run per check gives { messages, count }.
  • At most 200 runs start per check; the next check starts the rest.
  • Run in the designer starts one run with the newest failed message (the trigger's own state is not changed).

To answer a failure, follow the trigger with SAP CPI Monitoring (the message's attachments, the iFlow's deployed state), an email or a Teams message, or a Human task.

Settings

SettingDescription
SAP Cloud Integration (API) credentialThe tenant whose failed messages start the workflow (its key's roles: MonitoringDataRead). Required.
iFlowsTheir names, separated by commas; empty: all.
Also messages in RetryDefault: off.
Also escalated messagesDefault: off.
Look-back (minutes)Each check also reads this far before the last one (logs written late); a message still starts one run. Default: 2. Required.
RunsChoices: One run per message; One run per check with messages. Default: One run per message. Required.
Message variablee.g. {{ cpi.iflow }}, {{ cpi.messageGuid }}, {{ cpi.errorText }}, {{ cpi.logEnd }}. Default: cpi. Required.
RunChoices: At a regular interval; Every day; Every week; Every month; Advanced (cron expression). Default: At a regular interval. Required.
EveryDefault: 5.
UnitsChoices: Minutes; Hours; Days. Default: Minutes.
OnChoices: Monday; Tuesday; Wednesday; Thursday; Friday; Saturday; Sunday. Default: Monday.
AtHH:MM; several times separated by commas, e.g. 09:00, 18:00. Default: 09:00.
On dayMonths without this day are skipped. Default: 1.
Cron expressionminute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, e.g. "30 8 * * 1-5" = weekdays at 08:30.

Variables

VariableTypeDescription

cpi.messageGuidstringits message processing log id
cpi.iflowstringthe iFlow's name
cpi.iflowIdstring
cpi.statusstringFAILED, RETRY or ESCALATED
cpi.errorTextstringthe error (cut to 4000 characters)
cpi.logStartstringISO 8601
cpi.logEndstringISO 8601
cpi.correlationIdstring
cpi.applicationMessageIdstring
cpi.applicationMessageTypestring
cpi.senderstring
cpi.receiverstring
cpi.customStatusstring
cpi.linkstringthe message in the monitor

pages.title: Calls from Cloud Integration
pages.summary: An iFlow starts a Rail22 workflow through the Webhook trigger and an HTTP receiver adapter.
pages.html:
An iFlow can start a Rail22 workflow: the workflow starts with the core's Webhook trigger, and the iFlow calls the trigger's URL with an HTTP receiver adapter. No plugin step is needed for this.

  1. In Rail22, add a Webhook trigger, method POST, content type JSON (or XML as text), and choose its authentication: Basic auth or Bearer token fit Cloud Integration best. Save the workflow and copy the trigger's URL.
  2. In Cloud Integration, under Monitor > Manage Security > Security Material, add a User Credentials artifact with the user and password of the trigger (Basic), or a Secure Parameter with its token (Bearer).
  3. In the iFlow, add a receiver and connect it with an HTTP adapter: Address the trigger's URL, Method POST, Authentication Basic with Credential Name the User Credentials artifact. For a Bearer token, choose Authentication None and set the Authorization header (Bearer and the token) in a step before the adapter, such as a script that reads the Secure Parameter. Keep the secret in the security material, never in the iFlow.
  4. With Responds set to When the workflow ends, the iFlow gets the workflow's answer (200 with its state) and can use it; otherwise the trigger answers 202 at once and the workflow runs afterwards.

The trigger's HMAC-SHA256 signature authentication needs the iFlow to compute the signature of the body itself (a Groovy script): use Basic or Bearer unless you need it. The trigger's URL must be reachable from SAP BTP: a public address with a certificate Cloud Integration trusts (for a private CA, add its root certificate to the tenant's keystore).

pages.title: Requirements
pages.summary: What a server needs to run Rail22: PHP and its extensions, MongoDB, a web server, and optional tools.
pages.html:
Rail22 runs on a Linux server with PHP, MongoDB and a web server (nginx with PHP-FPM). On AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux or RHEL 9, the installer installs all of them. The installer (install.sh in the app's folder, or the setup in the browser) checks all of this before installing, and tells you what is missing.

Required

ComponentVersion / details
PHP8.1 or later, for the web server (PHP-FPM) and on the command line (/usr/bin/php, same version: the daemon runs the workflows)
PHP extension mongodb2.3.0 or later. The MongoDB PHP library ships with Rail22 (in app/pkgs).
PHP extensionsopenssl (encrypted credentials, TLS), mbstring, curl (HTTP and AI steps, OAuth), json, iconv, simplexml and zip (Excel import), ctype, session
PCRE10.30 or later, with Unicode (bundled with modern PHP)
Command-line PHP extensionspcntl and posix (the daemon)
MongoDBA server or replica set reachable from the app, with a database for Rail22. Knowledge bases need 8.3 or later (the installer installs 8.3).
Web servernginx with PHP-FPM, HTTPS
SMTP serverTo send emails: sign-in links, invitations, the Send email step

These folders must be writable by the app's user: the app's folder itself (the setup writes app.env there), logs, tmp, run and var.

Recommended

ComponentFor
PHP extensions zlib, bz2The FTP / SFTP steps: .gz compression, .bz2 decompression
curl with ftp, ftps, sftpThe FTP / SFTP steps (SFTP needs curl built with libssh)
gpg, openssl programsThe FTP / SFTP steps: PGP and S/MIME encryption and signatures
PHP extension ldapLDAP sign-in and the LDAP step. Rail22 has its own client when the extension is missing.
PHP extensions pdo_mysql, pdo_pgsql, pdo_sqlsrv or pdo_dblib, pdo_oci, pdo_firebird, pdo_odbcThe database steps: the extension of each kind of database, in the web and the command-line PHP. See Databases.
Node.jsInbound mail (Haraka) and the web browser tool server (Playwright)
systemd and polkitRunning the daemon and the other services, and managing them from Services (minimal systems may not have polkit: dnf install polkit)

Without the recommended parts, Rail22 runs. Only the steps that need them fail when used.

pages.title: Installation
pages.summary: Installing Rail22: the installer (install.sh) sets up the server and the app on RHEL 9 and its kin; or by hand, with the setup in the browser.
pages.html:
On AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux or RHEL 9, the installer sets up the whole server: the packages, the app's user, the app itself, the web server, and the options. Run it as root, from any folder:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/toolmk/rail22-core/main/install.sh
sudo bash install.sh

1. What it asks

  • The server: the site's domain (its DNS record points to the server), the system user Rail22 runs as (its home, such as /home/app, holds the app), and the repository and branch to install from.
  • Options: MongoDB on this server (otherwise you give the connection string of yours), a Let's Encrypt certificate (offered when the domain points to the server; otherwise a self-signed one), the web browser for the AI steps, inbound email and its domain, securing MongoDB (its own users with random passwords, sign-in required), and SELinux permissive when it is enforcing (nginx and PHP-FPM serve the app from the user's home).

It then shows what it will do and asks to go on.

2. What it does

  1. Installs the packages that are missing: EPEL, PHP 8.5 (Remi) with the app's extensions and the database steps' drivers (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Firebird, ODBC; Oracle's needs Oracle's Instant Client, installed by hand), nginx, MongoDB 8.3 (a MongoDB server already installed, such as Percona Server for MongoDB, is kept), Redis, certbot, and Node.js (the newest stream of the distribution; for the web browser and inbound email).
  2. With Percona Server for MongoDB on the server and its data folder still empty: turns on its encryption at rest, with a key file made for this server (/etc/mongod-encryption.key, readable only by mongod). Data written before cannot be encrypted in place: the installer says so and leaves it as it is (mongodump it, empty the data folder, run the installer again, mongorestore).
  3. Creates the user and its home, and clones the repository there, with its submodules (the libraries in app/pkgs).
  4. Writes php.ini (with the server's time zone), the app's PHP-FPM pool and the logrotate configuration (templates in scripts/system/), the certificate, and the nginx site.
  5. Sets up the app. It asks:
    • the database name (a new or empty one), and the MongoDB connection string when MongoDB is elsewhere;
    • the outgoing email: SMTP server, port, encryption (none, TLS, SSL), username and password, and the sender address;
    • the first account: the company or team, and its owner: username, email, first and last name, password.
    The app checks the answers itself: a wrong one, or a database that cannot be reached or already has an account, is asked again. It then creates the database indexes, the account with its roles (Owner, Member, Participant) and its owner, and writes app.env with a new random APP_SECRET.
  6. Installs the options and the background services (the workflow daemon, and Haraka and the web browser when chosen).

The firewall is not changed: open ports 80 and 443, and 25 for inbound email. Open the site and sign in with the owner you created. Run the installer again (sudo bash /home/<user>/install.sh) to update Rail22, to add an option later, or for Let's Encrypt once the domain points to the server: the app's settings and account are kept, and what is done is left as it is. It first offers to update the app's code from git when there are new commits on its branch (only when the app's files have no local changes; a fast-forward, nothing is reset), then starts again from the new code and updates what the parts install (Rail22's Haraka plugin, the services, restarted). When MongoDB's data folder has been emptied, or the app's database has no account, it offers to set the app up again (a new account; the old app.env is kept as app.env.bak-<time>). With the data folder, MongoDB's users are gone too: it turns sign-in off until it has made them again.

Warning: keep a copy of app.env in a safe place. Its APP_SECRET encrypts the stored credentials. Without it they cannot be read.

The app's folder

/home/app
  app/            the application (PHP); app/pkgs: the libraries (git submodules)
  public_html/    the web root (index.php, css, js)
  install.sh      the installer
  scripts/        its parts and the service scripts; system/: the templates
  etc/            links to the app's nginx site and PHP-FPM pool
  ssl/            the certificate (ssl.crt, ssl.key)
  logs/ tmp/ run/ var/    written by the app

Or: Docker Compose

On any Linux host with Docker: see Docker Compose.

Or: by hand

On another system, install PHP 8.1 or later with the required extensions, MongoDB, nginx with a PHP-FPM pool running as the app's user (see nginx and PHP-FPM), and polkit. Clone the app into the user's home with its submodules:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/toolmk/rail22-core.git /home/app

(In a clone made without --recurse-submodules, fetch them with git submodule update --init.) Write the nginx site (there is no app.env yet, so give the host name), then open the site: as long as there is no app.env, every address shows the setup wizard.

sudo scripts/nginx.sh install --server-name=netflow.example.com
  1. Prerequisites: the PHP versions and extensions (web and command line), PCRE, the writable folders, and the recommended tools. Fix what is marked as required, then continue.
  2. Server: the public address, the MongoDB connection string and database name (the connection is tested here, and the database must not hold an account yet), and the outgoing email.
  3. Account: the first account and its owner.

Then install the options and the services with the scripts below (on RHEL 9 and its kin, sudo bash install.sh does it: it keeps the settings the wizard wrote).

The installer's parts

After the server's packages, user, files and PHP-FPM, the installer runs these scripts, in this order. Each can also be run alone, as root:

ScriptInstalls
nginx.sh installThe app's nginx site and nginx itself (install; also setup, status, restart, ...; nginx and PHP-FPM)
playwright-mcp.sh installThe AI steps' web browser: Playwright MCP, its Chromium, its service and its entry in mcp.json (tool servers). Run it again later to add the browser to an installation without it.
haraka.sh installHaraka, for inbound mail, and its service (needs app.env). Also start, stop, restart, status, uninstall
mongo.sh secureMongoDB's users, then sign-in required in /etc/mongod.conf (security; needs app.env). Also users, auth, start, stop, restart, status
daemon.sh installThe daemon's systemd service, and the rule that lets the Services page control the installation's services (Haraka's and the web browser's too). Needs polkit.

The app's own setup (between the nginx site and the others) is app/v sys::install, run as the app's user. Then, as needed: the System AI, tool servers, and a super-admin.

Check

Run the check suite. It exercises the workflow engine, expressions, steps and integrations against your installation:

cd app/commands && ./CheckCommand.sh

It ends with all N checks passed, or lists what failed. Checks of services you have not set up (real FTP servers, an AI server) are skipped or fail, and say why.

pages.title: Docker Compose
pages.summary: Running Rail22 with Docker Compose: the containers, the settings, the browser and inbound mail options, the data's folders, upgrades and development.
pages.html:
Rail22 also runs with Docker Compose, on any Linux host with Docker Engine and its Compose plugin (2.24 or later). The images are built on the host from the repository; nothing is pulled but the base images. The installer remains the way for a server of its own.

Compose runs the app, its database and the web browser. HTTPS and mail are yours, the operator's: the site is published on 127.0.0.1:8080 for your reverse proxy, and inbound mail is your Haraka on the host (below).

The containers

ServiceWhat it runsStarted
mongoMongoDB 8.3, sign-in required from the start: its users (nfn_admin, nfn_app, nfn_haraka) are made at its first start, from scripts/mongo_users.js.always
appThe app: PHP 8.5 (AlmaLinux 9, Remi's packages, the same as the installer's) and PHP-FPM. At each start it creates the new indexes.always
daemonThe workflow daemon, from the same image. It waits until the app is set up.always
webnginx: the static files and PHP, plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1:8080, for your reverse proxy.always
playwrightThe web browser for the AI steps.profile browser

The script

All the Docker files are in docker/: the compose files, the images, env.example, the settings (docker/.env) and docker/docker.sh, which does the steps below:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/toolmk/rail22-core.git && cd rail22-core
docker/docker.sh install

install runs the setup (its questions below), builds the images and starts the containers. Step by step:

  • docker/docker.sh setup [--[no-]dev] [--browser | --no-browser] [--mail | --no-mail]: asks what an option does not say: development, the web browser, your Haraka on the host (--mail), the project's name (rail22-<the folder's name>: its containers, volumes and images, so two installations on one host stay apart), the containers' user (the folder owner's uid and gid, so root setting up another user's home gets that user), the data's folder (DATA_DIR: docker-volumes in that user's home, its folders made with their owners), the site's address and port (127.0.0.1:8080), the public address (the proxy's) and, with mail, the database's and the daemon's ports for Haraka. When .env exists, its values are the defaults (enter keeps them) and its passwords are never changed; otherwise it is written with random passwords. Without a terminal nothing is asked: the options, .env's values or the defaults are used. The compose files go in COMPOSE_FILE, so plain docker compose commands use the same ones. A port already in use here is reported. .env stays mode 600, owned by the folder's owner.
  • build [service...], start, stop, restart [service...], status, logs [service...], check (the check suite in the app container).
  • uninstall: the containers removed, the data kept; purge: the data's folders too, all data (it asks first).

It runs as a user of the docker group (or root). The plain docker compose commands on this page run in docker/ (cd docker), where .env names the compose files.

1. Settings

By hand instead: in docker/, copy the example and fill it in:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/toolmk/rail22-core.git && cd rail22-core
cd docker && cp env.example .env && chmod 600 .env
  • MONGO_ROOT_PW, NFN_APP_PW, NFN_HARAKA_PW: the database's passwords (NFN_HARAKA_PW: your Haraka's user), set before the first start. Use letters and digits only (they go into connection strings), for example openssl rand -hex 24.
  • HTTP_BIND, HTTP_PORT: where the site is published, for the reverse proxy: 127.0.0.1 and 8080. 0.0.0.0 only when nothing but your proxy reaches the port.
  • BASE_URL, SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT: the defaults of the setup's form; BASE_URL is the proxy's https:// address.
  • COMPOSE_PROFILES: the optional service, browser in the example (below); remove it to leave it out, and empty NFN_BROWSER_URL.
  • HARAKA_HOST, MONGO_HOST_PORT, DAEMON_HOST_PORT: your Haraka on the host, with compose.mail.yaml (below).

2. Start

docker compose build
docker compose up -d

Open the site (through your proxy) and finish the setup in the browser: the database's connection string is filled in already. The app writes app.env into the config folder of DATA_DIR, and the daemon starts. To set up without the browser, put sys::install's JSON in NFN_SETUP_JSON for the first start.

Options

The web browser

On by default: browser in COMPOSE_PROFILES and NFN_BROWSER_URL=http://playwright:8931/mcp. The app adds it to mcp.json at its start. Its container loads a firewall table before the browser starts (it needs the NET_ADMIN capability for this only, then drops every capability): the browser cannot reach private, loopback or link-local addresses, so neither the other containers nor the host. Then choose the accounts that may use it, in Account settings > Tool servers.

Reverse proxy

Your proxy holds the certificate and forwards to 127.0.0.1:8080. The web container trusts X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto from private addresses (Docker's networks: the host's proxy arrives from the bridge's gateway), so the app sees the client's address and HTTPS (secure session cookies). nginx on the host, the certificate from certbot:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name flows.example.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name flows.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/flows.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/flows.example.com/privkey.pem;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000" always;

    client_max_body_size 100M;
    proxy_read_timeout 600s;
    proxy_send_timeout 600s;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
    }
}

On RHEL with SELinux, nginx connects to the port only after setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1. Caddy instead, with its own certificate: flows.example.com { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 } (and request_body { max_size 100MB } for large uploads).

Inbound mail

The Email (inbound) trigger needs Haraka with Rail22's plugin (scripts/haraka/). The same Haraka relays the app's outgoing mail and signs it with DKIM. The keys, the DNS records and port 25 are yours, so Haraka runs on the host, not in compose:

  1. docker/docker.sh setup --mail: adds compose.mail.yaml, which publishes the database (MONGO_HOST_PORT, 27017) and the daemon (DAEMON_HOST_PORT, 9000) on the host's 127.0.0.1 for Haraka, and gives the app host.docker.internal (HARAKA_HOST, and the setup's SMTP server on port 25).
  2. Install Haraka on the host with the plugin and configuration of scripts/haraka/, and set in its config/nfn.ini: uri=mongodb://nfn_haraka:<NFN_HARAKA_PW>@127.0.0.1:<MONGO_HOST_PORT>/?authSource=<MONGO_DB>, job_host=127.0.0.1, job_port=<DAEMON_HOST_PORT>, bounce_dir=<DATA_DIR>/bounces. The repository's README.md (With Docker Compose > Inbound mail) has the commands and a systemd unit.
  3. Add the containers' addresses to config/relay_acl_allow (172.16.0.0/12, or the subnets of the project's networks: docker network inspect): the app's mail does not come from 127.0.0.1.
  4. DKIM: dkim/dkim_key_gen.sh <domain> root in config/dkim, then publish the TXT record it prints. DNS: the MX record of the inbound domain to this host.
  5. Set MAIL_INBOUND_DOMAIN in app.env (config in DATA_DIR) and docker compose restart app daemon.

Volumes

VolumeHolds
configapp.env (with APP_SECRET), plugins.json, mcp.json.
mongo-dataThe database.
logs, var, tmpThe app's logs, sessions and stored files, temporary files.
bouncesThe bounces your Haraka saves (its bounce_dir), which the app reads.
assetsFiles the app publishes for nginx to serve (public_html/assets).

Warning: keep a copy of app.env, in config in DATA_DIR (for example ~/docker-volumes/config/app.env). Its APP_SECRET encrypts the stored credentials.

Services, upgrades, commands

  • The Services page shows each service's state from its check (the daemon's port, the browser's MCP, your Haraka's port 25). Start, stop and restart them on the host: docker compose restart daemon.
  • Logs: docker compose logs -f daemon; the app's own log is logs/app.log in DATA_DIR.
  • Upgrade: git pull && git submodule update --init && docker compose build && docker compose up -d. The app creates the new indexes at its start.
  • The console: docker compose exec app app/v <command>, for example app/v check::run or app/v mcpserver::list.
  • Backups: see Backups and upgrades.

Development

compose.dev.yaml mounts the working tree's code over the image's (a change is live without a build), adds mailpit (the outgoing mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025; the setup's SMTP server is mailpit, port 1025), and publishes the site on 127.0.0.1 only. Set NFN_UID and NFN_GID to your own (id -u, id -g). The database is the mongo container's own.

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.dev.yaml up -d

pages.title: Configuration (app.env)
pages.summary: Every setting of the app.env file: addresses, database, email, security, limits, logging and the System AI.
pages.html:
Rail22 reads its settings from app.env in the app's folder. The installer (or the setup in the browser) writes it. Edit it to change a setting, then restart PHP-FPM and the daemon. The format is one NAME=value per line. Put a value in single quotes to keep it literal, for example a password with a $.

Warning: app.env holds passwords and the encryption secret. Keep it readable by the app's user only (chmod 600), and out of the web root.

Addresses and database

SettingDescription
BASEThe app's folder, e.g. /home/app.
BASE_URLThe public address, e.g. https://netflow.example.com. Links in emails, webhook and form addresses and the OAuth redirect URI use it, always as https://.
MONGO_URIThe MongoDB connection string, e.g. mongodb://user:password@db1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0.
MONGO_DBThe database name.

Outgoing email

SettingDescription
SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORTThe SMTP server.
SMTP_USERNAME, SMTP_PASSWORD, SMTP_AUTHIts sign-in.
SMTP_SECUREfalse, ssl or tls.
SMTP_AUTOTLSUse STARTTLS when the server offers it.
SMTP_DOMAINThe domain emails come from: noreply@<domain>, unless MAIL_FROM is set.
MAIL_FROMThe sender address of the app's emails and the Send email step.
SMTP_FROM_DOMAINThe name the app gives the SMTP server when it connects (EHLO). Empty: the server's host name.
ERRORS_EMAILWhere the errors of background jobs are emailed, besides the log. Empty: logged only.

Inbound email

SettingDescription
MAIL_INBOUND_DOMAINThe domain of the Email (inbound) trigger addresses. See Inbound mail.
HARAKA_DIRWhere Haraka is installed. Default: <app>/haraka.
DAEMON_PORTThe port the daemon takes its commands on, on DAEMON_LISTEN: the app and Haraka wake it when they queue a job (Haraka: job_port in haraka/config/nfn.ini, the same number). Default: 9000.
DAEMON_LISTENThe address the daemon listens on. Default: 127.0.0.1. Docker: 0.0.0.0, set by compose.yaml (the containers' private network only).
DAEMON_HOSTWhere the app finds the daemon. Default: 127.0.0.1. Docker: daemon. Haraka's is job_host in nfn.ini.
HARAKA_HOSTWhere Haraka listens, for the Services page's check. Default: 127.0.0.1. Docker: host.docker.internal, your Haraka on the host (compose.mail.yaml), which also turns inbound mail on (there is no Haraka folder to find).
PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_PORTThe port of the web browser for the AI steps, on 127.0.0.1, when scripts/playwright-mcp.sh install runs (it writes it into mcp.json). Default: 8931.

Security and behaviour

SettingDescription
APP_SECRETThe key that encrypts credentials and secret fields. Generated by the setup. Never change or lose it: stored credentials would become unreadable.
APP_DEBUGtrue shows error details on the pages and turns on development-only endpoints. Default false. Never true on a public server.
LOG_LEVELThe least severe messages written to logs/app.log: ERROR, WARN, INFO (default) or DEBUG.
HTTP_STEPS_ALLOW_PRIVATEtrue lets the HTTP Request and Download File steps call this machine and private networks (localhost, 10.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x…). Default false: public addresses only, checked again on each redirect. The integration steps that may reach on-premises servers (Bitdefender GravityZone, Veeam Backup & Replication, FortiGate, Sophos Firewall, Checkmk, Zabbix, Wazuh, VMware vCenter, Proxmox VE, Hyper-V) follow the account's own setting instead: see Account settings.

System AI

The AI server this installation offers to every account. See System AI.

SettingDescription
SYSTEM_AI_PROVIDERanthropic, openai, gemini, ollama, lemonade or lmstudio. Empty: no System AI.
SYSTEM_AI_URLEmpty: the provider's own API. Otherwise a proxy or your server.
SYSTEM_AI_API_KEY, SYSTEM_AI_MODELThe key and the model. Empty model: no System AI.
SYSTEM_AI_EFFORTClaude's effort (default high).
SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_INPUT, SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_OUTPUTUSD per million tokens. Needed for models whose prices Rail22 does not know.
SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITSThe credits every account gets each month (default 500, no rollover).
SYSTEM_AI_MAX_CREDITS_PER_REQUESTThe most one request may reserve (default 200; 0: no limit).

Other configuration files

Some settings live in PHP files of the app. Copy one to its .local.php name to change it: the local file is read instead, and updates don't overwrite it.

  • plugins.json, next to app.env: the plugins that are enabled and their settings (see Plugins overview), e.g. the Multi-tenant plugin's options (registration, system_ai), its plans (tiers: limits and features; without the plugin there are none: no limits) and the credits per model and the margin.
  • mcp.json, next to app.env: the tool servers.

Settings from the environment

DAEMON_LISTEN, DAEMON_HOST and HARAKA_HOST may also come from the environment, as Docker Compose sets them; app.env wins. NFN_CONFIG_DIR (environment only) is the folder of app.env, plugins.json and mcp.json: with Docker, config in DATA_DIR. Default: the app's folder.

pages.title: nginx and PHP-FPM
pages.summary: Serving Rail22 with nginx and a PHP-FPM pool, with HTTPS and the security headers.
pages.html:
The nginx site is a template inside scripts/nginx.sh, which fills it in (see below). The installer writes the PHP-FPM pool, php.ini and logrotate from scripts/system/; the app's etc/ folder links to the pool and the nginx site.

PHP-FPM pool

[app]
user = app
group = app
listen = /home/app/run/php-fpm.sock
listen.owner = nginx
listen.group = nginx
pm = dynamic
pm.max_children = 25
pm.start_servers = 5
pm.min_spare_servers = 2
pm.max_spare_servers = 10
slowlog = /home/app/logs/php-slow.log
php_admin_flag[log_errors] = on
php_value[session.save_path] = /home/app/var/php/session

The pool runs as the app's user, so it can write logs, tmp and var. Raise upload_max_filesize and post_max_size to the largest file you want to accept.

nginx

sudo scripts/nginx.sh install [--server-name=netflow.example.com]
sudo scripts/nginx.sh setup [--server-name=netflow.example.com] [--dry-run]
sudo scripts/nginx.sh start | stop | restart | reload | status | test | uninstall

install installs nginx when it is missing, writes the site and starts nginx (also at boot); setup writes the site again, after a change of the template or of BASE_URL. status shows nginx, the site (whether it is still as the template) and the certificate's end date; test runs nginx -t; uninstall takes the app's site out (kept as a .bak-<time> file) and leaves nginx installed. nginx is the server's: start, stop and restart apply to every site on it, other installations' too (restart and reload check the configuration first).

Writing the site fills in the template with the app's folder and the host name of BASE_URL (app.env; before the setup wizard has written it, give --server-name), shows the changes, and writes it to /etc/nginx/conf.d/<user>.conf, named after the app's user (or where the app's etc/nginx.conf link points). The old file is kept as <user>.conf.bak-<time> and put back if nginx -t fails; otherwise nginx is reloaded. --dry-run only shows the changes.

The certificate goes in ssl/ssl.crt and ssl/ssl.key of the app's folder. /etc/nginx/nginx.conf stays as installed: it loads conf.d/*.conf. The essentials of the site, with /home/app as the app's folder:

server {
    server_name netflow.example.com;
    listen 80;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
    server_name netflow.example.com;
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    ssl_certificate     /home/app/ssl/ssl.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /home/app/ssl/ssl.key;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    root /home/app/public_html;
    index index.php;
    client_max_body_size 100M;
    fastcgi_read_timeout 600;

    access_log /home/app/logs/app_access.log;
    error_log  /home/app/logs/app_error.log;

    # static files: long cache, compressed
    location ~* \.(jpg|jpeg|png|gif|ico|css|js|woff2|woff|eot|svg|ttf|map)$ {
        gzip on;
        expires max;
    }
    location ~* \.mjs$ {
        types { text/javascript mjs; }
        gzip on;
        expires max;
    }

    location ~ \.php(/|$) {
        try_files $uri =404;
        include fastcgi_params;
        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name;
        fastcgi_param HTTPS $https;
        fastcgi_pass unix:/home/app/run/php-fpm.sock;
    }

    # every other address: the app
    location / {
        try_files $uri @rewrite;
    }
    location @rewrite {
        rewrite ^/(.+)$ /index.php last;
    }

    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload";
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
    add_header Referrer-Policy "origin";
}

The app sends its own Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options and Permissions-Policy headers with each page.

Behind a proxy or load balancer

Rail22 takes the client's address from the connection. If another proxy is in front of nginx, list its addresses in app.trusted_proxies (app/config.php). Its X-Forwarded-For is then believed for sign-in limits and the audit log.

Logs

The app writes to logs/: app.log, daemon.log, php_error.log, and nginx's access and error logs. Rotate them, for example with etc/logrotate-qsm-app (weekly, 3 kept, or at 100 MB).

pages.title: Daemon and services
pages.summary: The workflow daemon, the systemd services, and the command-line tools.
pages.html:
Every run (Run in the designer, triggers, forms, human tasks, schedules, waits), human task time limits and outgoing emails are queued as jobs. The daemon runs them. Without it, no workflow runs and emails aren't sent.

Installing the services

sudo scripts/daemon.sh install
sudo scripts/daemon.sh start | stop | restart | rule | uninstall
scripts/daemon.sh status

It writes the daemon's systemd unit, starts it and enables it at boot. The other services have their own scripts, which write, start and remove their units:

UnitRunsWritten by
nfn-daemon-<user>.serviceThe workflow daemon (app/v.php daemon::run), as the app's user, logging to logs/daemon.log. Restarted if it fails.scripts/daemon.sh install
nfn-haraka.serviceHaraka, for inbound mail.scripts/haraka.sh install
nfn-playwright-<user>.serviceThe web browser tool server (see Tool servers).scripts/playwright-mcp.sh install

<user> is the app's user, e.g. nfn-daemon-app.service. It also adds a polkit rule that lets the app's user start, stop and restart these units, any other nfn-<name>-<user>.service of the installation and its nfn-haraka.service (even when installed later; sudo scripts/daemon.sh rule writes the rule again), so they can be managed from Services (see Administration).

Note: polkit must be installed first (minimal systems leave it out: dnf install polkit). Without it, the script stops before writing anything.

Several installations on one server

Each installation (for example a live one and a development one, each in its own user's home) has its own daemon and web browser: their units carry the app's user. Give each a different DAEMON_PORT and PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_PORT in app.env (for example live 9000 and 8931, development 9001 and 8932). Haraka listens on port 25, so only one installation runs it: scripts/haraka.sh leaves a Haraka unit written by another installation as it is.

The daemon's options

OptionDefaultDescription
--min-workers2Worker processes started at once and always kept.
--max-workers2 × CPUs − 1More workers are started while jobs wait. The extra ones stop after --idle-timeout (60 s) without work.
--max-per-accountmax − 1Running jobs of one account (0: no limit), so one account cannot take all workers.
--max-per-projectmax − 1Running jobs of one project (0: no limit).
--job-timeout0Seconds a job may run before its worker is killed (0: no limit).
--max-worker-memory256MB. A worker above it is replaced after its job.

A job whose worker dies or times out is queued again, and given up after 3 attempts. Given-up jobs appear in the account's execution log.

Command-line tools

Run them from app/ as the app's user, with ./v <command>:

CommandDoes
./v sys::run --id=<workflow>Starts and runs a workflow's draft.
./v sys::resume --id=<execution>Runs a sleeping execution again.
./v sys::indexesCreates the database indexes (after an upgrade).
./v sys::migrate [--dry-run] [--list]Updates the stored data for the new version (after an upgrade, after the indexes), such as a renamed expression function in saved workflows. Each migration runs once per database and is recorded. --dry-run shows what would change; --list shows every migration and when it ran.
./v sys::audit [--account=<id>]Checks the audit log's seal: changed, forged or missing entries.
./v demo::create --password=<password>Makes a demo account with realistic data (see Demo data).
./v demo::delete --account=<id>Removes a demo account made by demo::create.
./v MultiTenant::tiers::show [--account=<id>], ./v MultiTenant::tiers::setThe plans, and an account's plan, limits and usage (with the Multi-tenant plugin).
./v MultiTenant::admins::list | grant | revokeThe super-admins. See Administration.
./v MultiTenant::credits::show | add | plan | ratesThe accounts' AI credits (with the System AI option).
./v mcpserver::list | add | remove | enable | disable | testThe tool servers (mcp.json) and the accounts that may use them.
./v check::run [--only=…] [--verbose]The check suite (also commands/CheckCommand.sh).

In Docker

With Docker Compose the services are containers. The Services page shows their state from their checks and does not start or stop them: use docker compose restart <service> on the host.

pages.title: Inbound mail
pages.summary: Receiving email for the Email (inbound) trigger with Haraka: DNS, installation and configuration.
pages.html:
The Email (inbound) trigger needs the installation to receive email. Rail22 uses Haraka, a mail server on Node.js, with a Rail22 plugin. It accepts mail for the trigger addresses only, stores each message and starts its workflow. Without Haraka, the trigger is not offered (a workflow that already has one cannot be published) and Account settings has no Inbound mail tab.

1. DNS

Choose a domain for the addresses, such as in.example.com, and point its MX record at the server. Port 25 must be open to the internet.

2. Install Haraka

The installer does steps 2 and 3 when you choose Inbound email (sudo ./install.sh in the app's folder; run it again to add it later). Alone, as root (Haraka's files stay the app's user's):

sudo scripts/haraka.sh install --domain=in.example.com [--version=vX.Y.Z] [--dir=<folder>] [--dry-run]
sudo scripts/haraka.sh start | stop | restart | status | uninstall

It installs Haraka into <app>/haraka (or HARAKA_DIR), with the MongoDB driver, Rail22's plugin and configuration, then Haraka's defaults, and adds its service, nfn-haraka.service, started now and at boot (Haraka runs as root to listen on port 25). It never overwrites what is already there, except Rail22's plugin (plugins/nfn.js), which it updates when it changed: after upgrading Rail22, run it again. status shows the service, the inbound domain, the DKIM keys and whether port 25 listens; uninstall removes the service and keeps the files.

3. Configure

  • In app.env, set MAIL_INBOUND_DOMAIN=in.example.com.
  • Haraka's MongoDB user: when MongoDB's users exist (Security), its connection string is in app.env (HARAKA_MONGO_URI) and the install writes it into haraka/config/nfn.ini. Otherwise set uri there yourself.
  • Haraka wakes the daemon on 127.0.0.1, at job_port in haraka/config/nfn.ini (default 9000). When you change DAEMON_PORT in app.env, set the same number there.
  • Create DKIM keys for the domains mail is sent from through Haraka (the app's sender address, the forwarded aliases): cd haraka/config/dkim && ../../dkim/dkim_key_gen.sh example.com, then publish the TXT record it writes in example.com/dns. Haraka signs with the key of the sender's domain; a domain without a key is sent unsigned (more: haraka -h dkim).

4. Restart it

After changing its configuration: sudo scripts/haraka.sh restart (or from Services).

Addresses

Each Email (inbound) step gets an address <prefix>-<code>@in.example.com. The prefix is the account's, set by its owner on the Inbound mail tab of Account settings.

In Docker

Haraka is yours, on the host: compose publishes the database and the daemon on 127.0.0.1 for it (compose.mail.yaml), and the app reaches it as host.docker.internal. The DKIM keys and DNS records are yours too. See Docker Compose > Inbound mail.

pages.title: System AI
pages.summary: Offering an AI model to every account, paid with credits: provider, model, credits and rates.
pages.html:
The System AI is an AI model your installation offers to every account, so they can use AI steps and the Assistant without their own API key. Their use is paid in credits: a monthly allowance per account, plus top-ups.

Turning it on

The System AI comes with the Multi-tenant plugin, as its system_ai option (on as shipped, in its plugins.json entry: config). Set in app.env, then restart PHP-FPM and the daemon:

SYSTEM_AI_PROVIDER=anthropic
SYSTEM_AI_API_KEY='sk-ant-…'
SYSTEM_AI_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5
SYSTEM_AI_EFFORT=high
SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITS=500
SYSTEM_AI_MAX_CREDITS_PER_REQUEST=200

The provider can be anthropic, openai, gemini, ollama, lemonade or lmstudio. For a local server, set SYSTEM_AI_URL. For models other than Claude's, set SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_INPUT and SYSTEM_AI_PRICE_OUTPUT (USD per million tokens) so their use can be counted.

Then the AI steps of that provider list System AI as a credential, and the Assistant offers System AI as a provider.

Credits

  • Every account gets SYSTEM_AI_MONTHLY_CREDITS each month, or its plan's ai_monthly_credits. Unused credits don't roll over.
  • Top-ups add credits on top, valid for 12 months: ./v MultiTenant::credits::add, or a super-admin from the account's administration page.
  • Each call counts its tokens in credits, by the model's rate. A run reserves credits first and stops before a call once they are used up.
  • The rates per model and the margin are in plugins.json, the Multi-tenant entry's credit_rates.
./v MultiTenant::credits::show --account=<id>
./v MultiTenant::credits::add  --account=<id> …
./v MultiTenant::credits::plan --account=<id> …
./v MultiTenant::credits::rates

Accounts see their balance under Settings → AI credits.

pages.title: Tool servers
pages.summary: MCP servers the installation offers to the AI steps: mcp.json, the web browser, the accounts that may use them.
pages.html:
Tool servers are MCP servers that your installation runs (or reaches) and offers to the AI steps of the accounts you choose. Each run of an AI step that uses one opens a session, within the server's limits. Every installation has them; the first one most installations add is a web browser (Playwright, headless Chromium): the model can open pages, read them, click, type and fill in forms.

mcp.json

The servers are kept in mcp.json, next to app.env (not in git, readable only by the app's user: headers may hold tokens), in the shape other MCP clients use:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "search": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ..." },
      "label": "Search",
      "description": "Searches the intranet",
      "tools": ["search", "fetch"],
      "maxSessions": 4,
      "maxSessionsPerAccount": 2
    }
  }
}
FieldDescription
type, urlOnly HTTP servers (Streamable HTTP) are supported, not servers started by a command. The URL is called from the Rail22 server, so it may be on this machine or its network.
headersSent with each request.
label, descriptionShown in the AI step, and to the model with the server's tools (named <id>_<tool>).
toolsThe tools the model may use. Left out: all the tools the server lists.
maxSessions, maxSessionsPerAccountThe sessions at once on the whole installation (default 4) and per account (default 2).
serviceIts systemd unit, nfn-<service>-<user>.service, shown on Services.
managedByWritten by an installer (the web browser's: scripts/playwright-mcp.sh). The app shows and tests it, but does not change or remove it.

Edit the servers in the app (Tool servers: without the Multi-tenant plugin, the owners' tab of Account settings; with it, Settings → Tool servers for super-admins) or with ./v mcpserver::add. The file is read again when it changes. If it is not valid JSON, no server is offered until it is fixed.

Installing the web browser

sudo scripts/playwright-mcp.sh install [--port=<n>]

The installer runs it when you choose the web browser. Run it later to add the browser to an installation without it. It installs Playwright MCP, the Chromium its Playwright was built for (in /opt/playwright/browsers, shared by the installations of the server) and Chromium's system libraries, then the browser server as a service, and adds it to mcp.json as playwright with its safe tools (it leaves out those that run code or read the server's files). Then it runs a test. The browser server runs as its own user without a login, listens on 127.0.0.1:8931 only (or --port, or PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_PORT of app.env), and uses a fresh browser profile for each session. A firewall table stops it from reaching private, loopback and link-local addresses, including cloud metadata, so it reaches only the public internet.

sudo scripts/playwright-mcp.sh status | restart | uninstall

uninstall takes it out of mcp.json first. Chromium stays in /opt/playwright/browsers.

Giving accounts access

No account may use a server until it is switched on for it: by the account's owners on the Tool servers tab of Account settings, or, with the Multi-tenant plugin, by a super-admin on the account's administration page. Enabled accounts see the server under Tool servers in their AI steps. From the console:

./v mcpserver::list
./v mcpserver::test   [--server=playwright]
./v mcpserver::enable  --account=<id> --server=playwright
./v mcpserver::disable --account=<id> --server=playwright
./v mcpserver::add    --id=<id> --url=<url> --label=<label> [--tools=a,b] [--headers='{"Authorization": "..."}'] [--file=<an entry as JSON>]
./v mcpserver::remove --id=<id>

In Docker

The web browser is the playwright container (the browser profile), with its own firewall table. See Docker Compose.

pages.title: Administration
pages.summary: Super-admins: the accounts, plans and limits, suspending and viewing accounts; the installation's services; demo data.
pages.html:
An installation can host several accounts. With the Multi-tenant plugin, super-admins manage the installation and all accounts from Settings → Administration.

Super-admins

The super-admin flag is set only from the command line, never by a form:

./v MultiTenant::admins::grant --email=ana@example.com [--account=<id>]
./v MultiTenant::admins::list
./v MultiTenant::admins::revoke --email=ana@example.com

Super-admins must use two-factor authentication to open the administration pages. Every action they take is recorded in the audit log of the account acted on, and in their own.

Services

Services shows the installation's services (the workflow daemon, Haraka, the web browser) with their health, and lets you start, stop and restart them. Start, stop and restart need the services installed as systemd units, by their scripts (scripts/daemon.sh, haraka.sh, playwright-mcp.sh install).

Who sees it depends on the Multi-tenant plugin. With the plugin enabled, only super-admins do, with two-factor authentication, and the Administration pages link to it. With the plugin, it is Settings → Services. Without the plugin, the owners of the accounts do, on the Services tab of Settings → Account settings: on a single-account installation, the owner manages the server's services without a super-admin.

The installation

The Installation page shows the number of accounts, users, workflows and runs, the version, PHP and MongoDB, the server's load and free disk. It also shows the System AI. The tool servers have their own page, Tool servers (Settings menu, and a tab of the administration): add, edit, remove and test them (see Tool servers).

Accounts

The Accounts page lists the accounts with their plan, users, projects, workflows and runs of the last 30 days. Open one to:

  • Tier & limits: choose its plan, and change single limits or features for this account only.
  • Credits: its AI credits, plan and top-ups.
  • Tool servers: which ones its AI steps may use.
  • Suspend: its users are signed out at once, nothing new runs, and its queued jobs wait. Reactivate undoes it.
  • View as: see the account as its owner does, read-only and for a limited time, with a bar to go back.

Plans (tiers)

Plans set the limits and features of accounts. They come with the Multi-tenant plugin and are defined in plugins.json, next to app.env: the Multi-tenant entry's tiers. Without the plugin there are no plans: accounts have no limits, and the Usage tab shows no plan:

PlanData tablesRows per tableFilesAI credits / monthFeatures
Free31,000100 MB100none
Team50100,00010 GB2,000none
Enterpriseno limitno limitno limitthe installation'snone

Accounts without a plan get the default plan, Enterprise in the shipped file. Change plans with the Tier & limits panel or ./v MultiTenant::tiers::set.

Sign-up

With the Multi-tenant plugin's registration option on (plugins.json: the Multi-tenant entry's config), the sign-in page has a link to sign up: people can create a new account themselves. It is off as shipped.

Demo data

For a demo server, or to try Rail22 with realistic content, the console makes a demo account. Run it in app/commands as the app's user:

../v demo::create --password=<password> [--name="Northwind Supplies"] [--ai-from=<account id>]

Without --password it asks for one (at least 12 characters). It makes the account and five users who sign in with that password: nw.maria (the owner, who approves the requests), nw.daniel, nw.aisha, nw.tom and nw.elena. Their addresses are @northwind.example, which never receive mail. The project Finance holds:

  • the data table expenses with ten earlier requests and two saved views;
  • the workflow Expense approval, as in the guide Expense approval, published as v1, v2 and v3 with notes;
  • five runs started by its form over the last two days: four decided by Maria, one waiting in her My tasks;
  • three more workflows, with a manual trigger only;
  • with --ai-from: the Assistant and embedding settings of that account (on the same server), and the knowledge base Expense policy with five policy texts, indexed. Without it there is no knowledge base.

The emails of the runs fail: a running daemon sends them at once, to addresses that do not exist. The command prints the account's id. ../v demo::delete --account=<id> removes the account with all its data. It refuses an account that demo::create did not make.

pages.title: Backups and upgrades
pages.summary: What to back up, how to restore, and how to upgrade Rail22.
pages.html:
What to back up

WhatWhy
The MongoDB databaseEverything: accounts, users, workflows, executions, credentials, data tables, and the files (stored in MongoDB GridFS). Use mongodump, or your MongoDB backup tooling.
app.envThe settings and, above all, APP_SECRET. Without it, the encrypted credentials in a database backup cannot be read.
*.local.php filesYour own plans, credit rates and plugin list.
mcp.jsonThe tool servers and their headers.
plugins.jsonThe plugins that are enabled and their settings (e.g. the plans and the credit rates).
haraka/configIf you receive mail: its configuration and DKIM keys.
 
mongodump --uri="$MONGO_URI" --db="$MONGO_DB" --archive=rail22-$(date +%F).gz --gzip

Keep backups off the server, and keep app.env separate from database backups: together they give access to every stored secret.

Restoring

  1. Install the same Rail22 version and put back app.env and your *.local.php files.
  2. Restore the database: mongorestore --uri=… --archive=… --gzip.
  3. Run cd app/commands && ../v sys::indexes and ../v sys::migrate (a backup from an older version is updated to this one), then start PHP-FPM and the services.

Upgrading

  1. Back up, as above.
  2. Stop the daemon: sudo systemctl stop nfn-daemon-<user>.
  3. Replace the application files with the new version. Keep app.env, *.local.php, logs/, var/, run/ and haraka/. From git: git pull, then git submodule update --init, which brings the libraries in app/pkgs to the versions the new version uses.
  4. Create any new indexes: cd app/commands && ../v sys::indexes.
  5. Update the stored data for the new version: ../v sys::migrate. Add --dry-run first to see what would change. It runs only the migrations this database has not had; a failure stops it before the next ones, and it can be run again once fixed.
  6. Restart PHP-FPM and the daemon: sudo systemctl restart php-fpm nfn-daemon-<user>.
  7. Run the check suite: app/commands/CheckCommand.sh.

Warning: do not use git submodule update --remote. It moves each library to the newest code of its own repository instead of the version Rail22 was tested with.

With Docker

  • The database: docker compose exec mongo sh -c 'mongodump -u root -p "$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --authenticationDatabase admin --archive' > rail22.archive; restore with mongorestore the same way (-T: docker compose exec -T mongo ... < rail22.archive).
  • The settings: the config folder of DATA_DIR (app.env with APP_SECRET, plugins.json, mcp.json), and var (stored files), for example tar czf config.tgz -C ~/docker-volumes config var
  • Upgrading: see Docker Compose.

pages.title: Security
pages.summary: Hardening a Rail22 installation: secrets, database access, HTTPS, sign-in protection, agents and the audit log.
pages.html:
Secrets

  • Credentials and other secret fields are encrypted with APP_SECRET (app.env). Keep app.env readable by the app's user only, and back it up separately.
  • Secret fields are write-only in the app: after saving, they are never shown again, and they are masked in the audit log.
  • Workflows refer to credentials by name, so exporting or sharing a workflow exposes no secret.

MongoDB access

Turn on MongoDB authorization with separate users. The installer does it when you choose Secure MongoDB (offered while MongoDB is on the same machine and does not require sign-in yet). Alone, sudo scripts/mongo.sh secure, run as root while authorization is still off, creates:

  • nfn_admin (root), for operators. Its connection string is written to a file readable only by root: move it to a password manager, then delete the file.
  • nfn_app (read and write on the app's database), written into app.env.
  • nfn_haraka (only what inbound mail needs), written into app.env (HARAKA_MONGO_URI) and, when Haraka is installed, into its configuration.

The passwords are random and never printed. It then enables authorization in mongod.conf, restarts MongoDB and the app's services, and checks that the app signs in. users and auth do the two halves alone; status shows whether sign-in is required and whether the app signs in.

With Percona Server for MongoDB, the installer also encrypts the data at rest (while its data folder is empty), with a key in /etc/mongod-encryption.key.

Warning: keep a copy of /etc/mongod-encryption.key away from the server: without it the data cannot be read. It is a static key on the same server as the data: it protects the data files, their copies and old disks, not the data from the server's root. For more, keep the key in a key manager (Percona supports HashiCorp Vault and KMIP servers) and rotate it.

Web

  • Serve only HTTPS, with HSTS (see nginx and PHP-FPM).
  • Pages carry a Content-Security-Policy (scripts, styles, images and connections from the site only), X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and a restrictive Permissions-Policy.
  • Uploaded files are downloaded as attachments, never run in the app's origin. Only images are shown inline.
  • Keep APP_DEBUG=false. Errors then show only a reference, and the details go to logs/app.log.

Sign-in

  • Failed sign-ins and password reset requests are rate-limited per address and per email.
  • Owners can enforce two-factor authentication and set session limits per account. Super-admins always need 2FA.
  • A password reset ends the user's other sessions.

Outgoing requests

  • HTTP Request and Download File may call only public addresses unless HTTP_STEPS_ALLOW_PRIVATE=true. Each redirect is checked again.
  • The GravityZone, Veeam, FortiGate, Sophos Firewall, Checkmk, Zabbix, Wazuh, VMware, Proxmox and Hyper-V steps call only public addresses unless the account turns on Integrations may connect to private network addresses. Even then, they reach only private network ranges (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x, 100.64.x, fc00::/7): never this server's own addresses, loopback, link-local (such as 169.254.169.254) or reserved ones. On a server shared by several accounts, any account owner can turn it on: keep the Rail22 server's own network free of services that trust their callers.
  • The web browser tool server runs as its own user and is blocked from private networks by a firewall table.
  • Expressions and Code steps run in a sandbox (J): they can only read the run's variables, with time and step limits.

Agents

An AI step with tools acts on what a model decides, and the model reads text that an outsider may have written. To keep that safe:

  • Least privilege. Offer the tools the step needs. Write operations are not offered by default, and they ask for a person's approval by default when you offer them, as do project and MCP tools not marked read-only. The credential stays on the server, never in a schema, an argument or a result.
  • Account policy. Owners decide which integrations and write operations agents may use, whether writes always need approval, and a monthly budget (Account settings). It is enforced on the server when a step is saved and when it runs.
  • Limits. Each step can cap its tool calls, write calls and cost per run.
  • Prompt injection. Tool results, files and values from outside are marked as untrusted, with a random name per run, and the model is told they are data. This reduces the risk and does not remove it, so combine it with Lockdown after untrusted input, which sends every write for approval once the agent has read such content. Tool descriptions from MCP servers are not marked: only connect servers you trust.
  • Personal data. Mask personal data hides email addresses, phone numbers and IBANs from Claude, OpenAI and Gemini. It works by pattern and does not cover images.
  • Audit. Every tool call is a sealed entry in the audit log, with its arguments (secrets removed), result and approver.

Audit log

Audit entries are sealed. ./v sys::audit reports entries that were changed, forged or removed. Audit entries are kept at least one year.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.summary: How Rail22 is built: the PHP application, MongoDB, the daemon, plugins and the browser code.
pages.html:
Rail22 is a PHP application on its own small framework (V), with MongoDB as its database and plain JavaScript in the browser, styled with Bootstrap 5.

Parts

PartWhereWhat
Frameworkapp/sys/The V framework: routing, controllers, views, models (BaseModel), fields, sessions, hooks, the J language (sys/J).
Controllers, viewsapp/controllers/, app/views/<controller>/Pages and JSON endpoints, at /<controller>/<action>.
Modelsapp/models/Accounts, users, projects, workflows, executions, credentials, files, data tables. Each declares its schema: fields, types, permissions, rules.
Stepsapp/models/node/One class per step type (NodeApp*, NodeCore*, NodeTrigger*).
Utilitiesapp/util/Expressions, HTTP, email, formats, conditions, tiers…
Librariesapp/pkgs/Third-party PHP libraries, as git submodules pinned to a release or commit: the MongoDB PHP library, ReactPHP (event-loop, stream, child-process), evenement, php-asn1. Each is loaded through autoload in app/config.php.
Pluginsapp/plugins/<Name>/Optional features with their own models, controllers, views and commands, enabled in plugins.json (next to app.env), which also holds their settings.
Consoleapp/commands/, app/vCommands (./v <command>::<action>), including the daemon and the check suite.
Browserpublic_html/js/app.js (sidebar, theme, formatters), app.workflow.js (the designer), app.pjax.js (page loads without full reloads), forms, grids, editors.
Themepublic_html/css/theme.cssBootstrap 5.3.8 with Rail22's styles, built from SCSS.

How a workflow runs

  1. A trigger creates an execution (WfExecution): a copy of the version's steps and connections, with a token on the trigger.
  2. The execution moves tokens along connections. Each step's execute() returns the outputs to continue on, SLEEP to wait, or nothing (Merge waiting for its other inputs).
  3. Every run is queued as a job and run by the daemon's workers, also the ones started by people (Run, forms, tasks) and by webhooks. The web request wakes the daemon over its local socket, so an idle worker starts the run at once.
  4. A sleeping execution (Wait, human task) is saved with its wake-up time. The daemon resumes it then.

Multi-tenancy
